title: Demons storm home against Cats to claim AFLW prelim berth
text:
Melbourne has stormed home with the last five goals of the game to beat Geelong by four points in their AFLW qualifying final.

After Demons star Paxy Paxman put them in front with a snapped goal, Chloe Scheer marked and had a shot at goal for Geelong with 20 seconds left.

But the Geelong forward missed and the Demons won 8.8 (56) to 8.4 (52) on Saturday at Princes Park.

Melbourne kicked the only three goals of the last quarter after looking well out of the game in the third term.

Geelong onballer Georgia Prespakis was easily best afield in the first half, but Melbourne midfielder Liv Purcell helped spark the comeback and they had 34 possessions apiece.

It was the first time Geelong's Mick Stinear has gone up against his old club since the 2022 premiership coach left Melbourne at the end of last season.

Melbourne now has the week off, while Geelong's semi-final opponent will be the winner of Sunday's Sydney-Western Bulldogs elimination final.

The threat of lightning delayed the start of the game on Saturday by 10 minutes, but Melbourne's changeable spring weather meant much of the game was played in sunshine.

The Cats kicked clear in the second term, with four goals to one and led by 22 points at the main break. They twice led by 28 in the third quarter, before the Demons hit back.

With Purcell and 100-gamer Tyla Hanks leading the way, the Demons kicked four goals to three and cut the margin to 12 points at the last change.

Alyssa Bannan's accurate snap in the first 30 seconds of the final quarter brought the Demons to within a goal. Prespakis kicked a behind, then Bannan kicked her second.

Paxman put Melbourne in front for the first time since the first quarter with her goal at 17 minutes.

Two-time defending premiers North Melbourne are playing Carlton in the second game of Saturday's qualifying final double-header at Princes Park.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

title: Home battery subsidy scheme lauded despite government's search for cuts
text:
Environment Minister Murray Watt says he and all other ministers have been told to find savings in their portfolios, as pressure on the federal government to cut spending ramps up.

The RBA this week lifted interest rates for the fifth time this year, bringing the cash rate to an 18-year high and prompting the prime minister to commit to finding savings in the upcoming mid-year budget update [MYEFO].

Speculation continues about where savings will be found, with the prime minister telling the ABC that means-testing home battery or electric vehicle subsidies was not ruled out.

On Saturday, the Australian Financial Review reported Treasury is drafting options to cut back the home battery scheme, including lowering the subsidy available on the up-front cost of a unit.

Murray Watt says the Labor government is looking for savings across the board. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Senator Watt said where savings could be found was still under review through the Expenditure Review Committee [ERC], but lauded the Cheaper Home Batteries Scheme as "phenomenally successful".

"But again, we will be looking for savings right across government," he said from Brisbane, where he provided the government's weekly fuel supply update in place of the Energy Minister Chris Bowen, who is travelling to Türkiye for the COP31 climate summit.

" Every single minister in the government has been asked to find savings in their portfolios, just like we've been asked to do so in every budget update. "

Mr Bowen took to social media on Friday to celebrate 600,000 home batteries being installed since the program began in 2025.

The home battery subsidy scheme provides an up-front discount that covers around 25 per cent of the cost. (ABC News: Rhiannon Shine)

"They are also putting downward pressure on prices for everyone, whether or not you have a battery," he said in the post.

Changes to home battery rebates came into effect in May this year, in a bid to ensure the $7.2 billion scheme did not run out of money too quickly.

Opposition calls for subsidy to be scrapped

Dan Tehan says Labor needs to get "serious" about addressing inflation. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

Shadow Energy Minister Dan Tehan said the program, which he labelled "unsafe and unaffordable", must go.

"If Labor were serious about addressing inflation, they would simply scrap the subsidy altogether," Mr Tehan said in a statement.

Tip-offs allege solar battery rebate fraud Almost 100 whistleblower tip-offs claim dodgy operators are rorting a multi-billion-dollar taxpayer-funded solar battery program.

Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson was asked by reporters in Melbourne today whether the government should consider means-testing the home battery program.

"Our focus is getting rid of government programs that are stoking inflation right now; that's why we've put $31.3 billion in savings before the Albanese government," Mr Wilson said.

Echoing Mr Albanese and Finance Minister Katy Gallagher this week, Senator Watt accused the opposition of blocking "$10 billion of savings" currently before the Senate.

"On their logic, if they're saying that increased spending means higher inflation, then they are driving inflation higher by refusing to back in those savings that we've put forward," he said.

title: Lehmann says 'everyone' was ball tampering globally, denies Khawaja's sandpaper claims
text:
Former Australia coach Darren Lehmann claims ball tampering was once ever-present in international cricket, but denies Usman Khawaja's claim of widespread knowledge of the 2018 sandpaper plot.

Lehmann was the coach of the Test team during the Cape Town controversy, in which Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper to alter the condition of the ball during the match.

Bancroft, captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner were all suspended in the wake of the incident, while Lehmann stood down from his post.

Khawaja's explosive Sandpapergate claim Usman Khawaja claims all staff and players knew that the Australian team was using sandpaper to tamper with the ball during the 2018 tour of South Africa.

In an interview with Nine newspapers on the eve of the release of his new book, Sabr, Khawaja claimed Cape Town was not the first time the Australian side had used sandpaper to tamper with the ball and that the plan had been known by "all of us".

"Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us," Khawaja told Nine newspapers.

Speaking to ABC Sport's Summer Grandstand, Lehmann denied personal knowledge of the use of sandpaper and said he does not think all members of the Australian camp would have known about it either.

Lehmann did claim though that up until that day, "everyone around the world" was ball tampering.

Loading...

"I don't think everyone would have known [about the use of sandpaper]. You do know ball tampering is going on because it's been happening for 150 years," Lehmann said.

"It's just how it's being done, and how you would know to that extent? That's an individual case by case, to be fair.

"I can only speak to what I know, and I know ball tampering was a big part of the game of cricket. Now it is obsolete.

"That doesn't make it right either, but that's the case, and we paid a heavy price for that."

Khawaja said he had suggested to the entire playing group after Bancroft had been caught that they take collective responsibility.

Lehmann, who is part of the ABC's cricket commentary team and has recently joined the ABC Cricket Podcast as a co-host, said he could not confirm or deny that discussion took place, as he was not present.

Darren Lehmann stood down as Australian coach after Cape Town. (AP: Halden Krog)

"I don't remember that. There were two change rooms obviously, and there were meetings going on everywhere. To be perfectly honest I was in meetings with Cricket Australia a lot," Lehmann said.

"That could have been the case, I don't know. I'm not saying yes or no to that one. There will be different points of view everywhere on this whole matter."

Lehmann also said he was not aware of an alleged conversation between Bancroft and a member of the coaching team, which Khawaja said was important in the formation of the sandpaper plan.

Earlier on Saturday, a Cricket Australia (CA) spokesperson said they remained comfortable with the initial findings of their investigation.

"There has been a great deal of speculation in the eight years since the 2018 Cape Town Test, including extensive media coverage throughout last month's series in South Africa," the spokesperson said in a statement.

"During this time there has been the ongoing opportunity to present any relevant information, and this remains the case.

"All relevant information presented to CA to date has been properly considered and we remain comfortable with the findings of our integrity process."

Lehmann said the 2018 incident left him in a "really dark place" and said the release of Khawaja's book and its explosive accusations has brought up "bad memories" for him, the players and their families.

"End of the day, Cricket Australia had their findings. It was a really tough week, two weeks, at that time going through the process and talking to all the relevant parties," he said.

"I was in a really dark place for a period of time where for four months I didn't leave my house.

"Eight years after the fact and trying to sell a book is a bit different. That's Usman's choice and that's the way he wants to go.

"For the families and the people involved, I feel for them right now because it's taking them back to a really bad place. It's been eight years. You get to a place where you move on, and I've moved on with my life."

Darren Lehmann said the Cape Town affair left him "in a dark place". (AP: Halden Krog)

Lehmann said Khawaja had not reached out to him in advance of these claims going public.

"For me it's a really touchy one mentally, more than anything else, and I know the boys will be feeling that as well.

"Could he have said this at the time? I suppose that's one of the things in the book. I mean, books are there to sell.

"He's spoken to Pat Cummins apparently and the players. I haven't spoken to Usman, he hasn't texted me or rang me. That's just the way it is."

In 2021, Australia's Test bowling quartet of Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon released a statement denying any knowledge of the ball-tampering plan.

Speaking to SA Grandstand on Saturday morning, former Australian fast bowler and current South Australia coach Ryan Harris said he thought it was "a bit disappointing" that it had taken Khawaja "eight years to say that".

"That's probably all I want to say on that. Like most people, I've been interested to hear what the book is going to say."

Jason Gillespie, another former Australian fast bowler, said he had always "found it a challenge to believe" only three players knew of the plan, but would not suggest everybody was across it and backed the testimony of the bowling group.

"This is what was interesting, the umpires at the time studied the ball and said they couldn't see any evidence of ball tampering. That's what I find fascinating.

"And that's what the bowlers have come out and said, the actual umpires looked at the ball and found no evidence … of ball tampering."

title: Elders call for leadership to address Indigenous child safety crisis
text:
Complex problems require clear leadership, and few are more complex than safeguarding children from abuse.

A stream of media reports in recent months have highlighted how WA's child protection system has failed to address that problem, particularly for Indigenous children living around Port Hedland, where the state makes its riches.

In the weeks since, there has been little clear ownership of the underlying problems.

Child Protection Minister Jessica Stojkovski has made changes in Hedland, including appointing the state's most senior caseworker to oversee investigations and flying in more staff.

Jessica Stojkovski is WA's Minister for Child Protection. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

The problems go beyond her portfolio, and beyond Port Hedland, but one colleague has largely been trying to distance himself from the issues.

Leadership needed

Aboriginal Affairs Minister Don Punch insists he is working on these challenges behind the scenes, but says it's ultimately not his problem to solve.

"Aboriginal affairs is about managing a land estate, it's about negotiating compensation on native title, it's about heritage protection," he told ABC South West.

"The issues of welfare of Aboriginal people are a collective responsibility for the cabinet."

Don Punch has faced calls to resign over the crisis. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

Punch has finally agreed to visit the area after plenty of criticism from the opposition, although a date is yet to be set.

"What I went up there and saw was a community crying out for help, crying out for leadership," Opposition Leader Basil Zempilas said.

"The premier left them in the lurch and only went up very late in the piece, and still the Aboriginal affairs minister has not bothered fronting.

"He should be ashamed. He should quit."

Basil Zempilas says Don Punch has been missing in action over the crisis in WA's north. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

The minister of course rejected that idea and continued to point out that his portfolio "does not have a direct responsibility for housing or health or child protection".

Which is true. Each has its own minister responsible for an incredibly complex policy area.

But looking at the issue in that way risks treating the matter in the headlines as purely a child protection issue, which it isn't.

WA premier confronted by South Hedland community members Roger Cook was heckled in his first visit to the community since announcing a coronial inquest into the deaths of three local children.

Child protection generally gets involved with families when multiple things are going wrong.

Housing stress, homelessness, health issues including addiction, kids not attending school and family and domestic violence are some of the reasons.

Those issues are particularly acute for First Nations Western Australians.

The rate of Aboriginal children in care is some 19 times higher than the non-Aboriginal population.

The title "Aboriginal affairs" creates the perception, for some, that Punch is the man working across those parts of government to look after First Nations Western Australians, including those over-represented in the child protection system.

It's a perception helped by the state government's own website explaining that the portfolio is responsible for "managing and supporting Aboriginal welfare, heritage and culture".

'Passing the buck'

When Kariyarra elder Patricia Mason heard Punch distance himself from the current headlines, she called on him to quit.

"It's a game they're playing around each other in cabinet that it's not my responsibility, it's yours," she told the ABC.

"Passing the buck around that portfolio doesn't hold any weight for us as human beings."

Nymal elder Linda Doogiebee was similarly frustrated.

Linda Doogiebee is concerned about what the future holds for young Indigenous people. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

"We're going around in circles, and the impact here is about our Aboriginal children and the families," she said.

And that's the problem with responsibilities being divided without having a clear leader — those who need help don't get it.

Acknowledgement needed

Punch seemed to acknowledge that aspect of his role when parliament last sat.

"I am regularly invited to meet with traditional owners on country to listen directly to their concerns and discuss the issues affecting their communities, including the delivery of essential government service," he said.

"I work closely with ministerial colleagues whose portfolios directly affect Aboriginal communities, including the minister for child protection."

Don Punch says he works closely with his ministerial colleagues on the issue. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

But there have been few tangible examples he's been able to point to of him helping to resolve one of the most visible examples of Aboriginal disadvantage.

Instead, it's largely been about how it's not in his portfolio.

Elders call for royal commission, child protection minister's resignation The national Aboriginal children's commissioner has arrived in Port Hedland after reports of children living unsupervised in the Pilbara town sparked a political firestorm.

It was a similar story when he presented the government's annual Closing the Gap progress report to parliament this year.

It showed no change for WA in child protection, and the state going backwards on child development.

But none of that warranted a mention in his speech, which instead focused only on positive elements like new partnership agreements and an emergency ambulance services trial.

Important measures which should be celebrated, of course.

But given the scale of need and the cries for help coming from places like Hedland — and many others across the state — those living in the gap every day at least want an acknowledgement of the problem.

Listening key

Instead of seeing a minister take ownership of real challenges, community leaders say they see a minister shifting responsibility.

"It's creating so much concern for us as to wondering what's the future going to be for these young children that are in foster care and their parents," Doogiebee said.

After decades of broken promises about improving the lives of Aboriginal Western Australians, elders want leaders who will listen and offer a clear plan forward.

Premier Roger Cook was asked what those plans were when he visited Hedland last month, and what hope people should have that these long-standing issues will be addressed.

Jessica Stojkovski, Kevin Michel, and Roger Cook in Port Hedland. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

"We have teams working here, day in, day out, to keep the community safe and to work with them," he said.

"Kevin Michel, as the local member, works with community leaders on how best to configure and resource the services that we provide.

"But that's no different between this community and any other in Western Australia.

" There are always challenges and our role as the state government is to work with communities to address those challenges. "

The first step in working with those communities is ensuring people feel heard — whether by the Aboriginal affairs minister, or anyone else who can lead the charge within the halls of power.

title: Just 8 per cent of licensed pilots in Australia are women
text:
Western Australia's far north has long been a training ground for aspiring pilots, but women remain significantly under-represented in the industry.

The latest statistics from the Civil Aviation Safety Authority show women make up just 8 per cent of licensed pilots in Australia.

Western Australia's far north is a known hotspot for ambitious young pilots. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

Female pilots working in the Kimberley say greater visibility, networking opportunities and clearer career pathways could help encourage more women to take to the skies.

Shoal Air senior Broome pilot Caroline Jamieson said she was increasingly seeing the positive impact of women entering the traditionally male-dominated field.

Caroline Jamieson wants to see more women in the industry. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

"A lot of passengers actually end up asking me, 'Can I get advice for my daughter who is interested [in flying], do you mind if I get your number so she can reach out to you?'" she said.

"I think it's because they see us in this industry working and believe it is something they can do."

'Waiting for the girls'

Ms Jamieson said traditional gender stereotypes still come to the surface despite a slow increase in women entering the industry and changing attitudes.

Both Caroline Jamieson and Greta Taine fly to remote locations across the Kimberley. (Supplied)

She said sometimes passengers had initially mistaken female pilots for flight attendants.

"I would love some more girlfriends in the industry, I definitely encourage more girls to get into it, I wouldn't say it's [the gender imbalance] a negative thing," she said.

" It's growing, the girls are coming, we're waiting for the girls. "

Shoal Air senior Kununurra pilot Greta Taine said the camaraderie within the industry had helped create a positive working environment.

Greta Taine says she was lucky to grow up exposed to aviation. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

"I think everyone has a lot of mutual respect and we all band together. And being up here, it being so remote, you do have to look out for each other," she said.

" You come to work and it is mainly males, but at the end of the day they're your mates and we look out for each other. "

Ms Taine said young girls should not let their gender deter them from pursuing a career in aviation, encouraging anyone with an inkling to give it go.

"Lucky enough I had a family member who was in aviation so I knew the lifestyle," she said.

"It has its challenges but it's really rewarding. I just don't ever think if it was for this job I would have come to the Kimberley."

The six-seat Cessna 210 common in regional Australia is dubbed the LandCruiser of the sky. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

Industry representation

Australian Women Pilots Association vice-president and helicopter pilot Hilary Wilkins said building professional networks could help address the imbalance.

"Seeing people doing those jobs — you get on a plane from Perth to Broome and your captain is a female, that definitely helps," she said.

" Obviously to have a balanced workforce, you need some family friendly policies within the workforce and all of that together will add to the number of women in industry. "

In the Kimberley, aircraft almost serve as taxis, given the sheer size of the region, according to Ms Wilkins.

Hilary Wilkins says women face gender stereotypes in every industry. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

She said the remoteness gave newcomers vast opportunities to develop their skills.

"We do a lot of single-pilot operations. You have to make all the decisions on the day about where you're going, what you're doing, managing fuel, managing passengers," Ms Wilkins said.

"That stands people in good stead for when they potentially get into airlines and larger planes.

"But the other thing is in Broome, there's the opportunity to stay here and progress your career from small single-engine planes to twins, up to the bigger passenger aircraft."

Caroline Jamieson says parents often ask her for advice on how to help a daughter who wants to become a pilot. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

The federal government rolled out the Women in the Aviation Industry Initiative (WAII) in 2019, committing $8 million in funding to help increase female participation and retention in Australia's aviation sector.

This involved targeted programs in career pathways and professional development.

The Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts released a Strategic Action Plan in 2023, to map out the delivery of the WAII until 2026.

title: Inside the multi-billion-dollar industry of illegal peptides pushed by influencers
text:
Loading...

Social media pulses with influencers promoting peptides to fix any physical insecurity you might have. But most are not approved for human use and are sourced from a multi-billion-dollar black market.

Here, influencers explain why they push illegal peptides and we give you an exclusive look inside the unregulated Chinese labs where many are made.

When fitness influencer Josh Sawyer posts online about using unapproved peptides, hundreds of thousands of people watch.

One TikTok video documenting Sawyer’s first two months using unapproved peptide GHK-Cu has been viewed more than 415,000 times.

“If you’re thinking about starting GHK-Cu but you don’t know what to expect, let me break it down for you,” Sawyer tells his TikTok followers in one video.

The 22-year-old regularly posts videos documenting his use of GHK-Cu, which is widely promoted online for its supposed anti-aging benefits.

He's among hundreds of influencers on social media platforms who purport to be promoting fitness, health and wellbeing, while cashing in by pushing peptide products not approved for human use.

As of April 2026, more than 230 million views of TikTok content was linked with the hashtag ‘peptides', according to Australia's Alcohol and Drug Foundation, which aims to prevent and minimise harm caused by substance abuse.

Alongside this rampant promotion of unapproved peptides, health agencies are reporting an escalation in their use, leading to severe medical complications in some cases, and even death.

Loading...

Most influencers promoting illegal peptides are affiliated with businesses that sell them. ( )

Many influencers are promoting peptides that have not been approved for human use. ( )

Loading...

Many social media influencers advise followers which peptides to use and how to inject them, despite having no medical qualifications.

That does not seem to be a deterrent for millions of people around the world consuming tonnes of unapproved peptides promising everything from weight loss and wrinkle repair to rapid injury healing and muscle growth.

Bloomberg estimates the black market for illegal peptides is now worth up to $4 billion.

Peptides are short chains of amino acids that make up proteins in our bodies. Some are prescribed by doctors for legitimate medical use.

But unlike the peptides in legal medicinal and cosmetic products, Sawyer's favourite, GHK-Cu, is an injectable peptide that has not been approved for use by Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) and there is no assurance it is safe to use.

Josh Sawyer updates fans on his own use of the illegal peptide GHK-Cu. ( )

Influencer Josh Sawyer has thousands of followers on social media. ( )

Josh Sawyer tells fans what to expect when taking unapproved peptides. ( )

Promotion of unapproved peptides often targets young men and middle-aged women who are unhappy with their looks. ( )

As social media promotion of illegal peptides grows, reports of harm including serious kidney and liver damage, allergic reactions and severe dehydration, are rising sharply.

Last week, a coroner found that the death of Australian actor Richard Norton was "triggered by" his injection of unapproved peptides, and recommended the TGA consider tougher restrictions.



In the first six months of 2026, the Australian Poisons Information Centre recorded 345 cases involving unapproved peptides, more than three times the total for all of 2025.



In Canberra last week, the ACT government-funded Directions Health Service, which offers safe injecting equipment to drug users, reported it was running out of syringes due to the "enormous surge" in the number of peptide users seeking needles.



Earlier this year, seven Victorians were hospitalised with acute liver toxicity after using the illegal peptide retatrutide, which purports to aid weight loss, but has not been approved for therapeutic use or sale by any regulatory agency anywhere in the world.



Recent data from NSW Health shows 1,180 people visited emergency departments seeking treatment after taking unapproved peptides between July 2025 and September 2026.

A closer look at the NSW figures reveals the startling escalation of black market peptide use: in July 2025 the number of monthly emergency department visits linked to these peptides was 5; in September 2026 it was almost 220.

A NSW Health report reveals a stark rise in the number of emergency department presentations linked to unapproved peptide use. ( )

Young people accounted for almost 60 per cent of cases, with those aged 25 to 34 making up 32 per cent of presentations and 16 to 24-year-olds accounting for a further 25 per cent.

These groups are the most-active demographic user-base across major social media platforms globally, making them easy targets for influencers focused on physical aesthetics.

Posts about unapproved peptides, such as BPC-157, GHK-Cu, TB-500, retatrutide and CJC-1295, have attracted millions of views.

None has been approved by Australia's TGA for the injectable or therapeutic purposes promoted online, and the vast majority are made in unregulated factories overseas.

It is illegal to sell, supply, or advertise unapproved and unregulated peptides, and the TGA can fine and penalise social media influencers promoting such substances.

Packages of illegal peptides in China, ready to send to the billion-dollar black market. ( )

Loading...

Loading...

The contents of peptide vials ordered online cannot be guaranteed. ( )

The companies selling unapproved peptides online often present themselves as legitimate Australian businesses, openly list their products on websites and advertise them through social media influencer partnerships.

While they frequently include disclaimers on their sites, stating the substances are "not for human use" and are being sold as "research chemicals", these companies know individuals are buying them for personal use.

Some influencers remind their fans that they are not health experts, and are only talking about how effective the peptides have been for them personally.

But the popularity of figures like Sawyer, who knows he is breaking the law by promoting the illegal substances, shows the demand for black market peptides is soaring despite the risks.

Followers of the Adelaide-based influencer frequently message him asking what peptides to take and where to buy them.

Sawyer ends many of his posts about these substances with: "If you guys wanna get your hands on any of this stuff, link in my bio. Use code Josh10 for a discount."

Josh Sawyer says he's not worried about publicly promoting illegal peptides. ( )

When Sawyer first spoke with the ABC, he was working as an affiliate of Vital Peptides Australia, which sells peptides online that are not approved for human use.

One vial containing 50mg of GHK-Cu, when bought in bulk, costs less than $10; the same vial sold by an Australian distributor costs about $60.

In exchange for posting promotional content and giving followers a discount code, Sawyer was receiving free peptides and a commission from sales, which he says was up to $2,000 a week.

However, in the months after first speaking with the ABC, Sawyer says he heard from followers who bought products from Vital Peptides Australia that some received the wrong peptides, while others did not receive their orders.

Vital has to be a scam mate. I ordered and paid a month ago and still nothing. Stole my money for sure

Hey! I was wondering if you have heard from Vital Peptides at all? I ordered from them and paid and haven't heard anything. Worried they have been shut down

hey i bought from vital peps and used your code a few weeks ago how long do they usually take for you to get them

"Some were outright scammed … I just didn't trust them at all by the end of it," Sawyer says.

He says the company also stopped responding to his calls and messages.

ABC News Loop has attempted to contact Vital Peptides Australia several times, and has submitted questions for the business to answer. They have not responded to any queries from the ABC.

Sawyer has since aligned himself with another peptides company. While it does not publicly display product test results, he says it has a better reputation.

Although he promotes the peptides, Sawyer says he does not know where they are manufactured.

Loading...

People involved in the illicit trade say much of the supply flooding the black market originates in China, where unapproved peptides are manufactured in bulk in unregulated laboratories.

The ABC has identified more than 50 businesses claiming to sell peptides not approved for human use to Australians, with some using social media to promote their products.

Which is how Josh Sawyer came to be spruiking the alleged benefits of an illegal substance that hundreds of thousands of people are willing to pay for and inject into their bodies — without knowing what a vial truly contains and what it might it do to them.

The influencer economy

Sawyer first heard about peptides through social media personalities he followed online and from US podcaster Joe Rogan, who has spoken publicly about their alleged benefits on multiple occasions.

In one podcast episode, Rogan, one of the most popular online figures and role models idolised by young men, discussed the "benefits" of using peptides BPC-157 and TB-500.

Joe Rogan's podcasts and posts on Spotify, Instagram and YouTube have been heard and watched hundreds of millions of times. ( )

Loading...

Josh Sawyer says he takes GHK-Cu to maintain his youthful looks. ( )

When taken together, the BPC-157 and TB-500 combination is referred to online as the "Wolverine stack", after the Marvel superhero, because of claims it can accelerate recovery from injuries and boost muscle growth.

Despite neither peptide being approved for human use by the US Food and Drug Administration, the peptide combo is openly spruiked online by influencers, bodybuilders and athletes, and offered in bundle deals along with other illegal peptides.

Earlier this year, Sawyer began injecting GHK-Cu.

He believes it keeps his skin wrinkle-free and prevents hair loss.

"My looks matter," he says.

" A lot of the younger demographic are looking at things to improve their looks or muscle. "

Sawyer now injects the peptide several times a week.

The TGA has not approved GHK-Cu for human use, and there is no proof that it has anti-aging benefits when used as an injectable treatment.

As Sawyer's online following has grown, so has the number of people seeking his advice, despite him having no health or medical qualifications.

Josh Sawyer documents his use of illegal peptide GHK-Cu on his TikTok account. ( )

Peptides often escape border controls because they come in such small vials. ( )

Josh Sawyer injects himself with peptides. ( )

He has received hundreds of direct messages from followers, mostly young men, asking questions about peptides and what to use to improve their looks or gain muscle.

Some of the messages have concerned him.

"I had this kid who said he ordered with my code … and this kid sounded about 13 years old," he says.

Sawyer says people under 18 may have unrealistic expectations of what unapproved peptides can do and should not use them.

"There's no way they could possibly know enough … some of them don't understand that the results are pushed a bit further than the truth," he says.

"I said, 'Dude, I don't know if you've received your peptide yet. If you have, don't take it'."

But he has no hesitation in talking up peptides to his older followers, and recommending they order from his supplier.

"I figured if I take this stuff, I might as well get paid," Sawyer says.

He's not the only person the ABC spoke to who had the same idea.

Tracing the black market

"Reggie" claims to make millions of dollars from selling unapproved peptides. ( )

Reggie*, an operator behind a black-market peptide business, began selling in 2020.

"Look, the money's great. There's always going to be a market for this," he says.

The Sydney-based dealer says decided to start selling unapproved peptides after discovering a friend was using a website to scam people who were attempting to buy the products.

"I thought I'll just do what they do, but better and not scam people," he says.

What began as a small side business shipping a handful of orders each week eventually grew into a large-scale operation.

Peptide dealer "Reggie" says illegal peptides are flooding into Australia. ( )

Reggie claims that when business was booming he was processing up to 2,000 orders a week across Australia.

"At its peak, I was making about $150,000 a week," he says.

If sustained for a year, that would equate to almost $8 million. The ABC could not independently verify Reggie's claims about the scale of his operation or his finances.

He saw demand surge after legal and approved weight-loss drugs, such as Ozempic and Mounjaro, became widely known.

According to Reggie, many peptide sellers import unapproved products from overseas suppliers before reselling them through websites, encrypted messaging platforms and private online communities.

Loading...

Although the importation and supply of unapproved peptides is tightly regulated, Reggie says getting the products into Australia is "easy".

"The fact is, this stuff is going to continually flood into the country. You stop one [shipment], that's OK, 20 went through," he says.

Reggie says much of the supply originates in China, which is home to legitimate pharmaceutical manufacturers as well as businesses operating unlicensed facilities capable of manufacturing peptides at scale.

The ABC has identified a network of businesses in China that claims to manufacture peptides and sell them in bulk through Australian channels.

Loading...

Chinese-made peptides in boxes on the floor. ( )

Two vendors who communicated using encrypted messaging services provided the ABC with exclusive videos and images they said were recorded inside factories operating in two cities: Guangzhou and Shenzhen.

Both declined to provide the name of their factory but confirmed they were not licensed pharmaceutical manufacturers.

Loading...

Workers in blue plastic coveralls can be seen operating a conveyor belt system filling the vials individually before factory workers package and label a seemingly endless number of parcels to be shipped globally.

The videos show peptide vials are kept in storerooms with rubbish bins and are packaged on the floor by squatting workers.

"Peptides are very strict in China," a staff member claiming to work for the factory in Guangzhou said.

" If the company's information is exposed, it will be seized by the regulatory authorities, and the relevant personnel will face imprisonment. "

'We don't know what's in it'

Many social media users claim illegal peptide products have transformed their appearance, accelerated injury recovery or improved their overall wellbeing.

But Kara Joyce, a consultant pharmacist and lived-experience manager at the Butterfly Foundation, says there is little reliable evidence to back those claims.

She warns experimenting with drugs purchased from black-market suppliers comes with potentially deadly risks.

Kara Joyce warns that users cannot be sure what is contained in unapproved drugs ordered online. ( )

Testing has shown that peptides bought on the black market do not always contain what the buyer thinks they have purchased. ( )

"When you order something online, we can't be sure that it's actually been produced in a sterile environment," Ms Joyce says.

" We don't know what's in it, we don't know the dose, we don't know if it's contaminated. "

Ms Joyce says body image concerns are driving demand for these products.

"People are preying on vulnerable populations," she says, noting that young men and middle-aged women are key targets.

"I think it's a concern, particularly with young men who we already know are less likely to seek help if they have procured a medicine on the black market.

"We're also seeing a rise in women around perimenopausal and menopausal ages being targeted too."

She says these groups are particularly susceptible to online marketing promising anti-aging benefits and rapid physical transformation.

If you or someone you know needs help: Butterfly National Helpline — 1800 33 4673

Eating Disorders Families Australia — 1300 195 626

Eating Disorders Victoria — 1300 550 236

Eating Disorders Qld — 07 3844 6055

Professionals Credentialed in Eating Disorders

Lifeline on 13 11 14

Suicide Call Back Service — 1300 659 467

Kids Helpline — 1800 55 1800

MensLine — 1300 78 99 78

There are also growing concerns that people seeking illegal peptides are not being treated by qualified health professionals for underlying mental health conditions they may have.

"There could be people with undiagnosed eating disorders finding these medicines, using them, and it could trigger off worsening symptoms and they might not actually get the help they need," Ms Joyce says.

Sonya Weith, of Peer Qnect, a confidential helpline for people using performance enhancing drugs (PEDs), says the number of calls to the service from people using unapproved peptides, and from concerned family members, is rising.

Of great concern is that many callers do not know what they have taken.

"They know what they want from it … but they maybe don't know how it works in their body and what the risks are," Ms Weith says.

People injecting black market peptides have no idea what is really entering their body. ( )

Sonya Weith says the number of calls from parents worried about their child's use of peptides is increasing. ( )

In the first six months of 2026, Peer Qnect recorded 199 calls about PEDs. More than half were about unapproved peptides.

Ms Weith says that figure is increasing "exponentially".

"It can be really heartbreaking to hear these parents who are just really worried about their kids," she says.

Can test results be trusted?

Online peptide sellers frequently display certificates of analysis (COAs) as evidence that their products are safe and pure, as advertised.

COAs are issued by qualified laboratories following legitimate scientific testing.

Vital Peptides Australia, the company Sawyer was promoting when ABC News Loop first interviewed him, displays several certificates and provided copies to Sawyer as evidence that its products were legitimate.

But the ABC can reveal these certificates have been altered.

This report looks legitimate but it has been altered. ( )

Report numbers had been removed or hidden, and on at least one report, the report named a completely different business, which had commissioned the test.

A spokesperson for Janoshik, a legitimate European laboratory listed on the altered reports, confirmed the documents had been edited and deemed any company passing off reports in this way as being "untrustworthy".

"Falsified or edited reports unfortunately appear quite frequently in the industry," the spokesperson said.

Janoshik is commissioned to provide test results from clients globally.

Janoshik says some test result documents purported to have been provided by the laboratory cannot be trusted. ( )

The spokesperson says the company receives up to five reports a day where a test document has been altered or incorrectly used by a business that did not commission it.

"If customers notice that a report may have been falsified or edited … they should be cautious and verify it directly with the laboratory," the spokesperson advises.

If a customer cannot verify a report, it has likely been issued for a different company.

The spokesperson says Janoshik has contacted Vital Peptides Australia over the matter and has taken the case to its legal department.

Vital Peptides Australia did not respond to questions about these findings or a request to provide the ABC with a batch of products to be independently tested.

The crackdown

Authorities are stepping up efforts to disrupt the illegal peptide trade.

Joint operations involving the TGA, Australian Border Force and state police agencies have been established to target suppliers, importers and advertisers.

The TGA says those operations have resulted in the seizure and destruction of more than 94,500 unapproved peptide products this year.

Chris Bedford, an executive member of the federal government's Health Products Regulation Group, which includes the TGA and the Office of Drug Control, says the illegal advertising and importation of peptides has increased over the past 12 months.

"We don't have information on exactly how large the black market is, but we know it's growing," he says.

Chris Bedford says shutting down the illegal trade in peptides is an "ongoing challenge". ( )

Illegal peptides seized by the TGA during a raid. ( )

Unapproved peptides seized by Australian authorities. ( )

Authorities are cracking down on illegal, unapproved peptides. ( )

Unlike other illegal drugs, such as cocaine or methamphetamine, which are trafficked in kilogram amounts, a peptide vial may hold only a few milligrams, weighing less than a paperclip.

As each vial is about the size of an adult thumb, even bulk orders of unapproved peptides can be sent in small parcels that can move undetected through global mailing systems.

In June, the TGA made unapproved peptides a priority focus area, alongside unlawful weight-loss products, vapes and sunscreens.

The regulator said its response could include product seizures, infringement notices and civil or criminal penalties.

"We know that there's a significant opportunity for people to make money out of this and take advantage of vulnerable Australians," Mr Bedford says.

He says that since February 2025, authorities have removed more than 10,000 online advertisements, social media profiles and websites connected to the sale of unapproved peptides.

Peptides in boxes ready to be sent from China. ( )

But shutting down black-market sellers remains an "ongoing challenge".

Mr Bedford says operators can quickly reappear under new names after authorities remove their websites or social media accounts.

"Sometimes it feels like you remove one ad and then it phoenixes in a different form really, really rapidly after," he says.

AI tools and website-building software have made it even easier to create replacement storefronts, he says.

Authorities have begun targeting social media personalities involved in the trade.

In August, authorities seized more than $120,000 worth of illicit peptides and anabolic steroids from two homes in New South Wales allegedly linked to a social media influencer.

Police alleged the products were imported, relabelled and promoted online.

Influencer Josh Sawyer now promotes a different peptide distribution business. ( )

Sawyer says the crackdown does not concern him and that he intends to continue posting about unapproved peptides.

"I'd like to think that I'm less of a promoter and more just someone sharing my experience," he says.

"I've always figured if I do get into any trouble, it is probably going to be pretty insignificant.”

He argues his content is not advertising, describing it instead as educational material about his personal experience.

"If somebody is going to buy peptides, they're going to buy them regardless," he says.

"I would rather people get them through me."

Watch ABC News Loop's full investigation, Pushing Peptides: Inside the Black Market, coming soon on YouTube.

* Reggie is a pseudonym and he agreed to be interviewed anonymously.

title: Schoolgirl fighting cancer meets her idol Benson Boone
text:
Facing her second battle with cancer, northern NSW schoolgirl Kenzie Riddle only wanted one present for her 13th birthday.

And she got it last night when she met American singer Benson Boone on stage at his concert at the Brisbane Entertainment Centre.

In an emotional finale to Boone's first show in his Australian tour, Kenzie joined him on stage to perform his hit song Beautiful Things.

The dream became a reality for the year 7 Kingscliff student thanks to a video she filmed with her friends and Tweed singer-songwriter Fergus Hogan.

Kenzie said she was shocked to see the video had been viewed on Instagram more than 600,000 times.

"It was so much fun, and we just thought it would be really fun to get some publicity and meet him somehow," she said.

"I love his energy most of all, he is just super cool," she said.

"He's great at backflips; it's his signature move."

Fergus Hogan, 19, said he was contacted by one of Kenzie's teachers from the school he also attended.

"He told me about Kenzie's journey, and I was like, I'd love to help," he said.

"Benson Boone is an amazing artist and to give Kenzie a possibility of meeting him was easy for me and she is so deserving of it."

Singer-songwriter Fergus Hogan says he was approached to get involved in Kenzie's campaign by one of her teachers. (Supplied: Riddle family)

He said Kenzie and her friends came to the project with lots of ideas.

"They were a really nice group of girls, super supportive, and I think really excited about being on Instagram as well," he said.

'Sparkle' despite second cancer diagnosis

Mum Robyn Riddle said she was proud of her daughter's positive attitude in the face of her second cancer diagnosis.

Kenzie is undergoing treatment after being diagnosed with B-lymphoblastic lymphoma in September.

Four years ago, she was diagnosed with a different form of cancer in their home country of South Africa.

She went through chemotherapy and surgery before being declared in remission in January 2024.

Ms Riddle said Kenzie had been thriving since the family emigrated to Australia in March 2024, and community support since the new diagnosis had been invaluable.

"She's facing it head on," Ms Riddle said.

Kenzie is going through treatment for cancer for a second time. (Picture: Kenzie's Keepers)

"She's always had a bit of a sparkle in her eye; she is always very optimistic.

"We have a saying in our family, 'always shine your eyes', and she definitely does that."

title: Fishers' hurt on display as WA's demersal ban faces parliamentary scrutiny
text:
The first parliamentary scrutiny of Western Australia's demersal fishing ban has exposed deep ongoing divides over how the Cook government is managing the state's fish stocks.

Over three days of hearings this week, the Legislative Council's Environment and Public Affairs Committee heard from supporters and opponents of the ban, as well as the government officials tasked with enforcing it.

Along with closing the West Coast demersal fishery, Fisheries Minister Jackie Jarvis banned trawl fishers in the Pilbara, and halved other demersal fishery catches, aside from the Gascoyne fishery.

She pointed to the Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development's (DPIRD) assessment demersal fish like pink snapper, red emperor and dhufish were under 'severe threat' and the harsh rules were needed to protect the fish from extinction.

While conservation groups welcomed the move, it drew strong criticism from the recreation and commercial fishing sectors.

Manue Daniels says fishers are owed an explanation. (ABC News: Hayden Smith)

Distrust and frustration

The third day of this week's hearings cut to the core of the hurt and distrust within WA's fishing community.

Visibly emotional during her testimony, West Australian Fishing Industry Council (WAFIC) chief executive Manue Daniels told the hearing the government's approach needed to be scrutinised.

"Trust in fisheries management has been deeply shaken," she said.

"This inquiry can establish what went wrong, whether the decisions were justified and what must change so we don't find ourselves here again.

"WAFIC is not arguing against sustainability, we never have, but we expect decisions to be based on sound science."

The committee was told WAFIC had been writing to Fisheries ministers for at least 20 years raising concerns about persistent 'overfishing' of demersal fish on the WA coast by the recreational sector without response.

There were a number of protests across the state at the government's new demersal laws, including this former shark fisherman who chained himself to a government building roof. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Affordable shark off the menu

Fish retailers have told the ABC their businesses are failing as sales have plummeted and the price of fish increases.

Ms Daniels said fish were a publicly owned resource, and the government's decision to only re-open the West Coast demersal fishery to recreational fishers should be thoroughly examined.

"As commercial fishing access is reduced, we have made locally caught seafood increasingly difficult for ordinary Western Australian families to afford," she said.

Third generation shark fisher Nick Soulos spent 58 years operating in the waters off Bunbury.

He told the committee his entire fishing licence was cancelled in December, despite only half his fishery falling within the west coast bioregion.

Nick Soulos (right) and his shark fishing crew. (ABC South West: Jacqueline Lynch)

With shark forming 96 per cent of his catch, and never exceeding the required limit for associated scalefish catch, Mr Soulos said the government's decision was difficult to accept.

"(The fishery) put 200 tonne of shark into the domestic market, into the restaurants and fish and chip shops for the local consumers," he said.

Demersal fish have long been a popular catch for many anglers. About 130,000 people are licensed to fish from a boat in WA, about 70 per cent of them fishing in the West Coast demersal zone, which extends from Kalbarri to Augusta. (ABC South West: Madigan Landry)

"For the sake of 3 tonne of dhufish they have denied the consumer."

He told the committee it stood in stark contrast to the charter sector, which has been allowed to continue catching 25 tonnes of demersal fish each year.

Science resourcing questioned

The committee is probing fisheries management, as well as the impact of marine parks, renewable energy development and seismic testing.

Shark depredation, illegal fishing and other challenges to fish stocks are also being examined.

Every group which appeared was asked if it thought DPIRD was "adequately resourced to meet its responsibilities".

Many indicated they did not think it was, or that its priorities needed to change.

In a lengthy presentation, former WA Fisheries chief scientist Jim Penn said the department lacked both experience and expertise.

Dr Penn said his review of DPIRD's demersal stock assessment found multiple errors.

Kalbarri businesses hit hard by demersal fishing ban People in the coastal tourist town of Kalbarri say they are already suffering the effects of WA's demersal fishing ban, less than two months after it came into force.

"The review process did not take into account, or involve people that had the ability, to make those assessments, which is very unfortunate," he said.

But the department stood by its research and modelling during its appearance before the committee.

Director General Heather Brayford said stocks of demersal scalefish had not recovered to appropriate levels for two decades, with dhufish in a "worse situation" now than in 2006.

"Over that period the science has been accepted by various governments," Ms Brayford told the committee.

The ban came into effect earlier this year. (ABC News: Bridget McArthur)

"But getting decisions to effectively reduce catches has been difficult."

DPIRD's research was backed by the Conservation Council, which opposed attempts to "undermine" the science.

But the CCWA was also critical of the government; arguing the fishing industry was being held to a far stricter standard of marine protection than offshore oil and gas operators.

Questions still to be asked

Committee chair and Labor MLC Sandra Carr said this week's hearings were just the start of a lengthy inquiry.

She said she and the rest of the committee; Labor's Parwinder Kaur, Liberal Phil Twiss, National Rob Horstman and the Greens' Jess Beckerling, were approaching the issues in good faith.

Ms Carr acknowledged the emotionally charged nature of debate over the issue, and said running commentary from other politicians was not helpful.

Geraldton based MP Sandra Carr is chairing the inquiry. (ABC Midwest Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"We have to be mindful that there is a lot of emotion; anger, frustration, anxiety around it," Ms Carr said.

"And we have to deal with it, with the upmost respect, but caution as well.

"You called for the process; let it happen."

The committee aims to deliver its final report by June next year.

title: Triumph, tragedy and Alan Jones's drive to survive F1's deadliest era
text:
The motor racing world is mourning the death of Alan Jones, the 1980 Formula 1 world champion, who died on Thursday aged 80.

The Australian legend, a winner of 12 grands prix, leaves a huge legacy both on and off the track after a life dedicated to the sport.

As tributes flood in for Jones, and reflections of his tremendous career are written, his death has brought into focus the dangerous and deadly era of motorsport he competed in.

Jones raced and won in an era when the safety of drivers, marshals and spectators was not front of mind.

In an already dangerous sport, the period Jones raced in is often remembered much more for its tragedies than its triumphs.

And it was tragedies that had a major impact on Jones's career, right from the very beginning.

Jones begins F1 career at tragic Spanish Grand Prix

Alan Jones made his F1 debut at the 1975 Spanish Grand Prix, one of the darkest and most controversial F1 weekends in history.

Rolf Stommelen suffered serious leg injuries, while five spectators were killed when his car crossed the barrier. (Getty Images: Sutton Images/David Phipps)

There was drama from the start with fears barriers at the Montjuïc Circuit in Barcelona were not bolted in correctly.

Members of the Grand Prix Drivers Association went on strike before practice, but the race went ahead after alleged rumours that the Guardia Civil, Spanish law enforcement, would seize the cars, which were at the Montjuïc stadium.

Jones qualified 21st for Hesketh Racing, but would retire just three laps into the race after a collision.

But the horror of the day was still to come.

Race leader Rolf Stommelen went off the circuit on lap 26 due to a broken rear wing, with his Hill-Ford car crossing the barrier into the crowd.

Five spectators were killed and Stommelen was seriously injured. The race continued for another four laps it was called off.

The 1975 Spanish Grand Prix holds another slice of history, with Lella Lombardi becoming the first, and to this date, only female driver to score F1 world championship points after placing sixth.

Jones gets F1 drive after fatal accident

After falling out with Team Surtees at the end of the 1976 F1 season, Jones was out of the series for the start of 1977.

He would get his chance to return to F1 following a harrowing and tragic accident in South Africa.

Anthem mix-up fed Alan Jones legend Alan Jones's first F1 grand prix victory in 1977 was so out of the blue that he said the band played Happy Birthday to him instead of the national anthem, but is the story true?

Welshman Tom Pryce and a track marshal were killed in an incident that was indicative of the poor and unimaginably lacklustre safety measures of the day.

Renzo Zorzi, who drove for Shadow, suffered a fuel leak and pulled off to the side of the main straight at the Kyalami circuit.

A small fire broke out, leading to a pair of marshals running onto the track to extinguish the flame. One driver was able to swerve and avoid the marshals, but not Pryce, Zorzi's teammate.

Pryce was unsighted and drove at full speed into 19-year-old marshal Frederik Jansen van Vuuren, killing the teenager on impact.

Van Vuuren was carrying a massive fire extinguisher that hit Pryce in the helmet, killing the Welshman instantly.

Race winner Niki Lauda was preparing to celebrate on the podium, until a member of tyre manufacturer Goodyear was able to get to the Austrian and inform him of Pryce's death.

The horrific and needless deaths ultimately led to Jones being called into the Shadow team for the next race in the United States.

Later that year, Jones would claim a stunning maiden win in Austria, the only win Shadow ever achieved, which set him up for future glory in the years to come.

Jones 'turns down' Ferrari after double tragedy

From 1979 to 1981, Jones was at the peak of his powers.

Driving for Williams, he won 11 grands prix in those three years and claimed the 1980 world championship.

But things could have been much different had a potential move to Ferrari eventuated.

Ferrari had met Jones, telling him he was their second option if the famed Italian team could not sign Mario Andretti.

Ferrari missed out on Andretti, who went on to win the 1978 championship with Lotus, but the Scuderia instead signed Canadian Gilles Villeneuve.

Jones went on to sign with Williams, in what proved to be a formidable partnership.

But, as happened so often in motorsport, tragedy struck.

Ferrari suffered a pair of horrors in 1982, a year after Jones first retired from F1.

The remains of Gilles Villeneuve's destroyed Ferrari chassis, after his fatal crash in Belgium in which he was thrown from the car. (Getty Images: LAT Images)

Villeneuve died after a crash during qualifying for the Belgian Grand Prix, when he ran into the rear of a much slower car. Villeneuve's car launched into the air and he was thrown out as it crashed back to earth.

Didier Pironi suffered a similarly scary incident in Germany, suffering horrific leg fractures after running into the back of Alain Prost's unsighted Renault.

Jones claimed years later that Ferrari reached out to him to fill in for the final rounds of the 1982 season, but he took too long to reply and Ferrari chose another replacement.

F1 safety improves after Jones's retirement

In total, there were five drivers killed on F1 grand prix weekends during Jones's career.

Ayrton Senna, Roland Ratzenberger, and how the San Marino Grand Prix changed Formula 1 While the legendary Ayrton Senna took most of the spotlight, Roland Ratzenberger's legacy lives on through F1's safety innovations.

That does not include two drivers killed in F1 tests, as well as Australian Brian McGuire, who was killed at Brands Hatch in England in 1977 while driving an F1 car.

It was a horrifying era for Formula 1, but one that did improve in the years following Jones's retirement in 1986.

F1 went several years without a fatal incident, until a horrific weekend at the 1994 San Marino Grand Prix when Ayrton Senna and Roland Ratzenberger died in separate crashes.

There has been just one fatality in F1 since, when Jules Bianchi went off the circuit at Suzuka in 2014 and collided with a crane that was recovering the beached car of Adrian Sutil.

Several safety measures have been put in place, both on the race car and in how marshals and recovery vehicles enter the racing circuit.

The Halo, a curved, wishbone-shaped structure, now sits above the driver and has played its part in protecting drivers in several incidents, including Romain Grosjean's fiery 2020 crash in Bahrain, Lewis Hamilton being trapped underneath the wheel of Max Verstappen's Red Bull during the 2021 Italian Grand Prix, and Guanyu Zhou's frightening crash at Silverstone in 2022.

title: Musk axes Tesla's Cybertruck in favour of self-driving taxis
text:
Elon Musk says Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production next year after years of persistently weak sales for a futuristic model once touted as a rival to legacy pickup trucks.

The move is a major retreat from what has been one of Mr Musk's pet projects.

Mr Musk said the move would let Tesla make more of the Cybercab, a robotic taxi he has made central to the automaker's autonomous-vehicle ambitions, but one that has yet to prove itself commercially.

It has been a bruising week for Mr Musk, as his record political spending of nearly half a billion dollars yielded little in US midterm elections, with most of the Republican candidates he backed losing their races.

Combined, his companies were on track to lose more than $180 billion in market capitalisation for the week.

Mr Musk called the Cybertruck the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made". (Supplied)

While it was not immediately clear whether Cybertruck production would move to another facility or be phased out entirely, the automaker's Austin plant is the only known Tesla facility equipped to manufacture the specialised components for the heavy, angular model.

In response to a user on X, Mr Musk called the Cybertruck the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made" and the wind-down the "end of an era".

Tesla has been shifting its focus to robotics and autonomy, a transition analysts say comes at the expense of the electric-vehicle business it helped pioneer as Chinese rivals gain ground.

The US EV maker began delivering the Cybertruck to customers in late 2023.

SpaceX's initial public offering revealed the also Musk owned company bought a fleet of cybertrucks. (Supplied)

According to automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the company only sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down 48 per cent from 38,965 in 2024.

Around the start of production in 2023, Mr Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 units.

"It doesn't make sense to keep it going when it's not meeting its targets," said former Aston Martin CEO Andy Palmer.

"Every rational auto guy would say the same.

" It will no doubt only be a rounding error on Tesla's balance sheet, but the statistics speak for themselves. "

Mr Musk's SpaceX was one of the model's biggest customers last year and bought Cybertrucks worth $131 million from Tesla in 2025 at list price, according to its IPO filing.

'Cybertruck won't go, can't go'

Right from its unveiling in 2019, the Cybertruck was a controversial choice for Mr Musk.

Pickup truck purists mocked its angular design, and safety experts predicted it would be hard to gain approval for sale in key markets like Europe.

Elon Musk attempted to demonstrate Cybertruck's bulletproof nature, only to leave the model with two huge cracks. (AP: Ringo H.W. Chiu)

The unveiling event was marred when Mr Musk tried to prove its windows were shatterproof by having metal balls thrown at them—only to leave massive cracks in two.

During Cybertruck's official launch in 2023, Mr Musk touted it as a futuristic competitor to pickup trucks from General Motors and Ford, saying "finally, the future will look like the future".

But the model has struggled to live up to those expectations.

Tesla has issued 11 recalls for the Cybertruck since it went on sale in late 2023, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration.

Some vehicles required physical repairs, while others were fixed with over-the-air software updates.

Automotive analyst Felipe Munoz said that although the Cybertruck has been called a failure because of its poor sales, electric pick-ups from Ford and others have also flopped in the US market.

"All of them lost the competition because electric pickups aren't popular in the US," Mr Munoz said.

But Cybertruck's sharp-edged stainless-steel design limited its prospects in markets like Europe, where EVs are more popular.

Regulatory approval was impossible for Europe because of rules there concerning pedestrian impact.

"Anywhere where you have crash regulation that takes into account pedestrian impact, that Cybertruck won't go, can't go," Mr Palmer said.

Musk's new bet

The Cybercab, which has butterfly doors and no steering wheel, pedals or mirrors, is one of Musk's key bets in his push to turn Tesla into an AI and robotics company rather than just an automaker.

Mr Musk has said he sees it as Tesla's main autonomous model supplying a global network of robotaxis.

After years of delays to Mr Musk's self-driving targets, Tesla began offering paid rides in a small fleet of Cybercabs in Austin in September.

However, the automaker still has to answer the US auto safety agency's questions on whether it has properly self-certified Cybercab to demonstrate compliance with federal motor vehicle safety standards.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened an audit in September to review the basis for that certification.

"Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab," Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said.

Elon Musk has a lot to lose at US midterms as pollsters tip blue wave As the US midterm elections approach, the trillionaire SpaceX and Tesla boss is making an expensive foray back into politicking.

However, the Cybercab is unlikely to make up for lost Cybertruck volumes soon.

The two-seater robotaxi is still a small program, with production beginning only earlier this year.

Tesla has listed an installed capacity of more than 125,000 units.

About 570 of the more than 1,200 Tesla robotaxis operating in Texas are Cybercabs, with the rest mainly Model Y vehicles, according to the state's Department of Motor Vehicles.
