title: Mixed picture for retail as three David Jones Perth stores set to close
text:
At least three David Jones stores in Perth are set to close after the retailer this week entered receivership, as a mixed picture emerges of the future of retail stores across the metropolitan area.

The Westfield Carousel, Garden City and the Karrinyup DJ stores are all likely to shut, according to investment analysis firm MST Marquee.

The fate of its CBD flagship is also uncertain, with landlord Starhill Global REIT's flagging a reduced footprint for DJ in the Hay Street Mall building or an entirely new tenant.

The company's flagship CBD store. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

But the news comes in the same week Morley Galleria shopping centre reopened after a $240 million upgrade, banking on strong suburban retail demand.

The optimism of that investment stands in stark contrast to the reality for David Jones.

Uncertainty over Perth store

Starhill Global confirmed in an announcement to the Singapore Stock Exchange this week that David Jones in the city was $1.48 million behind in rent.

"It's troubling. It is troubling for everyone who is concerned," City of Perth Lord Mayor Bruce Reynolds said.

Bruce Reynolds says there is uncertainty for the retailer. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"There's uncertainty, we don't know what's happening, and ultimately, our thoughts are for those who are going into Christmas not knowing what's ahead."

Former employee John Flood said he felt sad for affected staffers.

John Flood is a former David Jones employee. (ABC News: Mya Kordic)

"One of my first gigs as Santa Claus was at David Jones just up the road here and I loved it," he said.

"So it's a little sad I suppose. I feel, as well, for the staff and the people."

People lined up outside David Jones in Perth's city centre for the Boxing Day sales in 2013. (ABC News: Hayley Roman)

Starhill Global said it was considering whether to get a replacement tenant or open the building to multiple tenants, and reducing David Jones' floor area.

Hope for CBD retail

The company said it remained upbeat about the medium to long-term business outlook for the Perth CBD, though.

Working at David Jones was 'heaven on a stick' Former staff say years of cost cutting and reduced staffing has taken a toll on the experience of shopping at David Jones.

It pointed to "the opening of the Edith Cowan University City Campus in February 2026, continued population growth and supportive economic fundamentals in Western Australia".

But Lord Mayor Reynolds acknowledged in the short-term, it was challenging for the retail sector with many empty shopfronts in the city.

He was hopeful some of the more notable empty spaces would fill again.

"If you look at St Martin's Arcade, which has a lot of empty spaces at the moment, that has been closed and vacated for a quarter-of-a-billion-dollar investment," he said.

"And that will be re-imagined into a five-star hotel and new retail."

The Perth CBD David Jones store pictured around 1979. (Supplied: State Library of Western Australia/Richard Woldendorp)

He said the Carillon site was still waiting for some "green shoots" to anchor tenants into that space.

"Once that happens, then you'll be looking at another hotel within the mall," he added.

"Vacancy after vacancy, we'll see that to start to return. That's going to take time and it's going to take investment.

"In the last four months alone we've had $800 million invested in the CBD area around people that do have confidence in the state of the future of the City of Perth," Lord Mayor Reynolds said.

At the same time, the state's peak business group stressed big retailers like David Jones played an important role in the business environment of a city or major suburban shopping centre.

The CCI says big retailers like David Jones are important to the business. (ABC News: Zahra Anwary)

"This attracts foot traffic and that supports smaller retailers so they can be competitive and they have the customers they require as well for their businesses to flourish," Chamber of Commerce and Industry (CCI) chief economist Dr Daniel Kiely said.

Besides the impact of online shopping, David Jones customers had their own views on why the 188-year-old business was in so much trouble.

Paul Loiterton is the owner of a coffee shop on Bayview Terrace across the road from Claremont Quarter, which houses David Jones, and said its business model was "outdated".

Paul Loiterton thinks the David Jones business model is "outdated". (ABC News: Zahra Anwary)

"Take Claremont, for example, every concession in David Jones also has a store in this shopping centre. Why are they doubling up?" he said.

Dannielle Tilly said she did not have a good experience in the store.

"I just think, as I work in customer service, you'd have to know your product," she said.

Danielle Tilly (right) says she hasn't had much help on the rare occasion she's been to the store. (ABC News: Zahra Anwary)

"I just don't think they have enough staff that know the details of the store."

Trading hours debate

The CCI also put it down to what it called "some of the most restrictive trading hours across the nation".

Where to now for David Jones? Can you be in administration and have receivers? Yes, and it is happening at David Jones, which is seeking to restructure but will likely face challenges.

It again called for trading hours to be extended on Sundays and public holidays.

Lord Mayor Reynolds said there should be "a national urgent conversation around the future of retail".

"I've been in business for 30 years and I can tell you from that experience it's never been harder to run a business than it is at the moment,' he said.

"So what we can do in order to make people have the opportunity to become more profitable from an organisational and a countrywide point of view, they're conversations that are urgently needed."

title: Wool trade shortage sees producers, shearers become wool classers
text:
After four weeks of study in a classroom that is anything but typical, a motley crew of outback students have received their wool stencil.

Shearers, stock agents, wool handlers and wool producers have learnt how to categorise wool in terms of colour, strand, fineness, texture and style.

It is an essential skill in the shearing shed.

"Today, they're doing their final exam," Anna Ingold, a wool classing teacher from TAFE NSW said.

"They get a 3-kilogram bag of wool with smaller pieces in it that they have to sort by uniformity in regards to micron length and strength, and find any faults within the wool."

The number of wool classers in Queensland has effectively doubled. (ABC Rural: Crispian Yeomans)

Wool quality retained amid trade shortage

Australia produces 25 per cent of the world's wool, which is sold at auction in Sydney, Melbourne and Fremantle near Perth before being mostly shipped overseas for processing.

But different qualities can fetch different prices, which is why a classer is needed to categorise the shorn wool.

Skye Agar says she wishes industries would use wool more. (ABC Rural: Crispian Yeomans)

Wool producer Skye Agar, whose family won champion flock fleece at the Brisbane Ekka this year, drove seven hours from Barbara Plains Station, near Wyandra, for the training at Longreach.

She said understanding the processing and pricing of wool was "enlightening".

"It's just really good knowledge to have being a wool grower [to understand] the whole process after shearing," she said.

"Because as a grower, usually your job is just to get the sheep to the shed and then away from the shed."

A wool-classing cohort has completed its final exam after a decade without a pathway. (ABC Rural: Crispian Yeomans)

Queensland shearer David Grant said wool classing was non-negotiable because without someone to grade the wool, it could not be sold.

" Occasionally you'll get a bit of a hiccup at work and you'll lose a classer or something, once the classer has gone out of the job, the job just stops. "

Mr Grant said he decided to learn wool classing as a "backup" after decades in the industry.

'Bare minimum' but industry recovering

Longreach grazier Mike Pratt, who also chairs the Queensland Wool Technical Advisory Group (WoolTAG), organised the training to meet a wool trade shortage.

He said there has not been a wool classing "pathway" in Queensland since 2013.

"The industry has operated on the bare minimum, that is, if a classer gets sick, it's almost impossible to find a replacement," Mr Pratt said.

Mike Pratt says the training was organised with help from the Queensland government and TAFE NSW. (ABC Rural: Crispian Yeomans)

He said Queensland needed "about 10" more classers and only had 12 shearing contractors operating in the state, or "down from a hundred when wool was king".

"Wool is bringing rewards for those people [still] in the industry, like a good clip would average $3,000 a bale, which is potentially double what it would have five years ago," he said.

"So we're looking pretty good, and we need to make sure it's sustainable and make sure we've got the right workforce coming through for this wool harvesting industry."

The rise and fall of Queensland's wool industry It's been 30 years, but sheep country in western Queensland is fighting to bring the wool industry back.

Wool has faced stiff competition from synthetics and cotton, particularly as the wool industry has historically marketed merino to high-end fashion markets overseas.

The market has been relatively strong lately but has declined by $2 a kilogram since the new financial year, after a dramatic $7 rise since 2025 that reinvigorated the industry.

But Ms Agar said wool was a "brilliant" fibre and "incredibly versatile".

"It's great for extreme activewear because its incredibly antibacterial and it's a natural fibre, so it's good to wear and it keeps you warm and cool," she said.

"I just wish people, industry would use it more."

The 15 graduates will need to lodge accreditation with the Australian Wool Exchange before they can begin using their new skills in shearing sheds across the country.

title: Moving house seven times in 18 months the reality for many renters
text:
Frances Thiele has moved seven times in the past 18 months.

Bouncing between share houses, the 61-year-old disability support worker has struggled to find an affordable rental in the regional city of Albany, about 450 kilometres south of Perth.

"There just isn't anything," she said.

"The cheapest place I found for one person was $500, and that's half of my week's wages."

In Western Australia, rent inflation is at record levels, with new research from Anglicare showing essential workers are essentially locked out of the private rental market.

Renters in Albany are being priced out of the housing market. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Just one property across WA's two most populous regions, the Great Southern and South West, was within budget for key workers in health and childcare sectors, according to the charity's annual rental affordability snapshot.

Ms Thiele's precarious housing situation comes despite working full time.

"The job I do doesn't make money from people — it's not a job that'll ever be highly paid," she said.

" I do it because I feel useful, and I feel like I'm helping the community. "

Rising costs have forced her into shared housing, where she splits $850 a week in rent with a housemate.

The 61-year-old splits $850 a week in rent with another housemate. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

"It's easier to get a big house because these are hard to rent out as no-one can afford them," she said.

"With two wages, it just makes it much cheaper for us."

No room to grow in the Pilbara

Further north in WA's Pilbara, employers say they are now forced to compete with mining and energy giants to find staff somewhere to live.

Clark Smith says lack of accommodation means he cannot expand. (ABC Pilbara: Amy Rossbach)

Clark Smith runs a small mechanical workshop in Karratha, 1,530 kilometres north of Perth and said accommodation shortages were stopping his business from growing.

"I could put three guys on tomorrow and not even make a dent in the work we've got," he said.

" I would expand in a second, but I just can't. "

Mr Smith used any available option to house workers.

"I've put people in mates' houses … we've had people staying at the yard in caravans," he said.

"I've had staff houses, three or four guys in it, which at the end of the day, living and working together is not healthy either."

Clark Smith (right), with employees Brad Wild and Jayden Crute at his Karratha workshop. (ABC Pilbara: Amy Rossbach)

Karratha has been Mr Smith's home for 17 years and accommodation had always been a challenge.

"We lived in a van with no air con through a couple of months of the summer, wherever you could get," he said.

"In five years, we lived in 10 different houses."

Small businesses struggle to compete

Many roles offered in Karratha included housing and a car, something small business owners found difficult to match.

"All of them know that, at the drop of a hat tomorrow, they could go work for a company and earn twice as much and have a roof over their head," Mr Smith said.

"I can't compete; it's physically impossible to compete."

Clark Smith has turned to multiple methods to house staff amid Karratha's accommodation shortage. (ABC Pilbara: Amy Rossbach)

One employee of Mr Smith's was living in affordable housing, as part of a scheme supported by the City of Karratha and industry partners.

Mr Smith said the scheme was helpful, but it came with limitations.

"You're only allowed one per business, and if she gets a pay rise, they get kicked out of their housing because you have to earn under [a certain] amount," he said.

Loading...

Other employees have had to move between houses or relied on relatives to stay in Karratha.

"I've got a 22-year-old who still lives at home … he doesn't have a choice," Mr Smith said.

"It's very hard to make this place a home because of the accommodation situation."

Part of the roof collapsed at Powerhouse Parramatta on opening day. Anthony Segaert

title: Usman Khawaja remained silent for eight years. Why did he speak out now?
text:
Advertisement

SportCricketTest cricket Opinion Usman Khawaja remained silent for eight years. Why did he speak out now? Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist November 7, 2026 — 4:09pm

November 7, 2026 — 4:09pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australian cricket has itself to blame for the eight-year suppurating wound that has been reopened by Usman Khawaja’s memories of the South African tour of 2018. It bled in 2021 when Cameron Bancroft gave the interview that sealed his fate as an Australian representative. Former Test batsman Usman Khawaja has opened old wounds with his recollections of what occured in Cape Town, South Africa, in 2018. Dan Peled David Warner and his manager periodically reopened it. Left unhealed, it was always ready for a new bleed. If they’re looking for their beloved “learnings”, Cricket Australia, and Australia’s Test players, might look back to their failure in 2018 to honestly and broadly tell the truth about what happened at Newlands and on that tour.

Advertisement

Their window of opportunity for truth-telling lasted about a day, when they could have accepted collective responsibility and tried to bring the rest of the cricket world with them. Instead, they attempted to ring-fence the blame around Bancroft, Warner and Steve Smith, to punish those players and hope the heaviness of those punishments would be a substitute for treating the wound. As any battlefield surgeon could have told them, all they were doing was creating the conditions for a long-term recurrent infection. Their missteps started, but never finished, with that oldest of cricketing and human motives: looking after number one. Khawaja is right when he says his three teammates were scapegoats for a responsibility that should have been shared.

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘It was all of us’: Khawaja blows the whistle on more sandpaper use in South Africa in 2018 Did the bowlers know Bancroft took a specific piece of sandpaper onto the field at a specific time? No; we can take them at their repeated word. But they have not answered the question they are being asked, which is whether they knew, more broadly, that their team was altering the ball, as many other teams had done for decades, to enable reverse swing. The plausible deniability scheme – ask no questions, hear no lies – doesn’t wash. It didn’t wash for Smith, who as captain said he didn’t want to know the specifics. He paid the price for his dereliction of leadership. But it didn’t wash for the team, either.

Advertisement

Thanks to reverse swing, they won matches and series as a team, they reaped rewards as a team, they built a reputation as a team. Yet when the crunch came, Bancroft and Warner were isolated as individuals and only Smith was made to take wider responsibility. Why didn’t Khawaja speak earlier? His explanation, that he wasn’t asked, is only a partial defence. Cameron Bancroft was the most junior of the banned trio. Artwork: Maria Ercegovac He had every opportunity to reveal what he knew, behind closed doors, to Cricket Australia, and he chose not to. He, like everyone else, was looking out for number one. The only person who failed to look out for number one was Bancroft, through his naivete, implying in 2021 that the bowlers knew about the ball-tampering. He never played for Australia again.

Advertisement

The behaviour and treatment of Warner repeated it again and again. Look after number one because the collective won’t have the guts to step forward. Khawaja is accused of making his revelations now so that he can profit by selling books. Then newly sacked Australian cricket captain Steve Smith addresses the media at Sydney Airport in 2018, after arriving back from the ball-tampering scandal in South Africa. Janie Barrett Anyone who knows the first thing about books is laughing into their teacups. Khawaja has received his advance, he was well paid as a cricketer, and books aren’t that profitable. (Ask Warner, who prefers to protect his ongoing lucrative employment than throw it all away for the pyrrhic satisfaction of “selling books”.) Khawaja remained silent for eight years for the same reason everyone else did: it wasn’t in their personal interest. Now he wants to get it off his chest. It’s a bit late but it’s also about time someone was open with their version of the truth.

Advertisement

The fact that he’s waited for post-career, when he has less to lose, underscores the centrality of self-interest. Newlands offered a rare opportunity for Australian and international cricket. Ball-tampering, both contemporary and historic, could have been admitted and acknowledged. There was a chance for truth-telling and cleansing. This isn’t hindsight speaking. Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith face the media in Cape Town 2018. Getty Images On the day the scandal broke, many of us idealists pleaded for cricketers collectively to show a moral courage akin to the physical and mental courage they displayed on the field. It turns out that this would have been Khawaja’s preference, too. But instead of saying “me too”, past and present players united under a different response: me first. And here’s where it ends up. Damage reopened, friendships rebroken, families re-traumatised, cricket re-vandalised. It didn’t need to be this way but Cricket Australia and its players set the tone on day one.

Advertisement

If you’re not going to cauterise this wound, get set for a long, slow bleed. Improbably, it still isn’t too late. Khawaja has been brave, if belatedly. The members of that team and their staff need only admit that they consented, implicitly if not explicitly, to dirty tricks because they thought such tricks were endemic in Test cricket. That’s all Khawaja has done and all he is calling for: a bit of team spirit. Fat chance?

Advertisement

Maybe nothing has changed since Darren Lehmann’s first press conference as coach of an Australian team shamed by losing games. What was his responsibility? “To win,” he said, with one of those smiles that hinted that if you don’t understand it’s about winning, you don’t understand anything. It turned out that there was a bigger shame than losing, a shame with a long life that still has years to run. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday. title: Kevin Morby on being half of alt-country’s power couple
text:
“Now that I’m a bit older, I understand that time doesn’t have to be an enemy,” says Kevin Morby.

The singer-songwriter – who just welcomed a baby with his partner, Waxahatchee’s Katie Crutchfield – embraces change on his new album, Little Wide Open.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

There’s a new kid in town at Kevin Morby’s house. He hasn’t been there long, but he has changed the lives of the 38-year-old and his partner of almost a decade, fellow singer-songwriter Katie Crutchfield, who makes music as Waxahatchee. The two became parents to a baby boy three weeks before this interview, and everyone is asking Morby how he’s handling the lack of sleep. “And I have to tell them that we’re actually all sleeping fine,” says Morby. “The baby is really chill, but I feel weird about telling people that. I have a couple of other friends who just had children this year as well, and they aren’t getting much sleep, and I feel like they don’t want to talk to me. They kind of hate me.” Morby is speaking from the family’s mid-century ranch house in Kansas City – the couple divide their time between there and Los Angeles – ahead of an Australian tour behind his latest album, Little Wide Open. He wrote the songs when he and Crutchfield were contemplating their future, and he was aware his life was about to change. It made him think about time and his relation to it. “On my previous album, This Is a Photograph, which I love, it felt like being in a boxing ring with time, waiting to be knocked out. But now that I’m a bit older and making some big life decisions, I understand that time doesn’t have to be an enemy. It can be your companion if you’re on this trip together with someone.” Morby’s journey to this moment has had some definite turning points. He had a transient childhood, moving house multiple times due to his father’s job with General Motors. He was born in Lubbock, Texas, then the family shifted to Detroit, then Tulsa, then Oklahoma City, before settling in the suburbs of Kansas City. As a teenager, he suffered panic attacks.

Advertisement

“There were a couple of years in high school of just living moment to moment, terrified of when the next attack was going to happen. I eventually dealt with them through meds at first, and then a really good therapist, and I started eating more healthily and riding a bike all the time, which helped.” He also started playing music and joined a band, but it was when he played his first solo show at a bookstore that he had an epiphany, “because I couldn’t believe how cathartic it was. It was like finding this enlightenment, and it felt like a huge weight off my chest. It was exhilarating.” Morby with Katie Crutchfield of Waxahatchee, his partner of almost a decade. The couple welcomed their first child in July. Getty Images for The Recording Academy Soon afterwards, at the age of 17, he dropped out of high school, and after saving $600 from a job in an Indian restaurant, he got on an Amtrak train and moved to New York with a suitcase, a sleeping bag, his guitar and a four-track tape machine. He lucked out by scoring free board at a home in Brooklyn’s Carroll Gardens in exchange for babysitting. It was 2006, and he immersed himself in the vibrant music scene that was blossoming in Brooklyn at the time, seeing Jeffrey Lewis, Kimya Dawson, Dirty Projectors, TV on the Radio and more. Morby and Crutchfield had a meet-cute in 2012 while both playing on the same bill – at the merch table she undercut him on the price of a tour t-shirt to a prospective customer. They kept crossing paths on tour over the years and became friends, eventually getting together in 2017. Fans love dissecting their songs to decode whether they are writing about each other, none more so than the 2024 Waxahatchee breakout track, Right Back To It, an affecting ballad about keeping a long-term relationship alive, where Crutchfield duets with MJ Lenderman.

Advertisement

“I actually listened to it again yesterday when it came up randomly on a playlist and thought ‘Goddamn that’s a great song!’” says Morby. “There’s certainly a back and forth between us, where it feels like some of the songs are talking to each other. On this new album, I’ve been jokingly saying that I made it more Americana so Katie can really hear it and get into it.” In a recent interview, Crutchfield said, “it’s a strange situation to fall in love with an album that’s also kind of about your life.” The new song Bible Belt was inspired by a tragedy. A couple were on their way to see Morby play in Denver in 2021; they never made it. Their car was involved in a crash – the girl was badly injured and spent a long time in hospital; her boyfriend died. When Morby heard what had happened, he made contact with her. “I wrote Bible Belt in the back of the tour bus after hearing that news,” he says. “A year later, I’m in Paris and playing the Bataclan, where the horrible shooting happened in 2015. And I look down from the stage and there in the front row is this girl and she’s with her boyfriend’s mother. They said it was important for them to be there. Like a symbol, you know? “Touring can be a slog. You’re travelling a lot and trying to figure out where to eat and where to take a shit and you’re tired all the time. But then there are moments like that, when you realise there are people who have gone through hard times or tragedies, and in some small way you’ve helped them through. And that’s an honour.”

Advertisement

Sometimes the honour goes the other way. In 2016, Morby released a stand-alone protest song called Beautiful Strangers. It referenced Bataclan, along with the Pulse nightclub mass shooting in Orlando, Florida, and Freddie Gray, who died while in police custody in Baltimore in 2015. It’s a song about remembrance, solidarity and strength in the face of prejudice, brutality and violence. Years later he got a call telling him that the legendary gospel and soul singer Mavis Staples wanted to cover the song. It ended up on her most recent album, Sad and Beautiful World, and won the 86-year-old a Grammy for Best American Roots Performance. “I mean, this is someone Bob Dylan idolised,” he says. “She marched with Martin Luther King. She’s a historical figure. Everything she’s done in her life is just unbelievable. And here she is covering my song. “When we finally met, it was like being in the presence of greatness. And she said, ‘Kevin, you went to the other side of the mountain, and you wrote Beautiful Strangers, and you came back and gave it to all of us.’” He shakes his head. “It’s the most amazing thing that’s ever happened to me... Besides Katie and my son, of course,” he quickly adds, smiling. Kevin Morby’s Little Wide Open is out now. With his clerical collar, black blazer and sunglasses, Monsignor Alberto Rocca cuts an imposing figure as he walks past the stark white of the Powerhouse Parramatta’s steel exoskeleton. And he should. Rocca holds a lot of power: he’s the gatekeeper of the Codex Atlanticus, a collection of 1119 pages from Leonardo da Vinci’s notebooks dating from 1478 to 1519, and the man responsible for delivering a small selection of the artist’s drawings from Milan to western Sydney. Monsignor Alberto Rocco at the Powerhouse Parramatta on opening day. Audrey Richardson Standing in the dimly lit room that houses the drawings, Rocca explained just what it takes to move the pages – which are so delicate, each page can only be displayed for three months at a time – safely to the other side of the world. “When you transfer important masterpieces you have a codified method, which is international,” he said.

Advertisement

The works are sealed in Milan in clima frames, a specialised, protective framing system that controls humidity, before they are placed in special crates to help keep the temperature low while they are on a plane. When the drawings arrived in Parramatta, Rocca said they were placed in showcases that have technology to allow for the temperature and light to continue to be controlled. “Light is very dangerous for drawings,” he said. “If you have some paper in your house and you put it under the sun for two days, it fades.” Monsignor Alberto Rocco stands in front of where the da Vinci drawings are displayed. Audrey Richardson While he’s explaining the importance of protecting the drawings from light, a news crew with a camera light on walks in, illuminating the dark room. He stops speaking and frowns, saying “this is very bad”. He looks relieved when they leave. The papers are part of Task Eternal, the museum’s flagship exhibition that unpacks humanity’s fascination with stars, flight and space. The da Vinci drawings of flying machines were transferred from Veneranda Biblioteca Ambrosiana – an institution that’s more than 400 years old. Rocca is director of the library’s art gallery.

Advertisement

Related Article City life Visitor’s guide to the new Powerhouse Parramatta It’s a strong contrast to the newly opened Powerhouse Parramatta, which the Catholic priest praises for its design and large exhibition space. Although he’s been to Sydney before, it’s his first time visiting Parramatta, and he said it was a nice feeling to see the drawings on display in a new environment. “When we have da Vinci and we have great masterpieces, they are world patrimony, and so for us to be here, it is also a way to share and to make also people in Parramatta to understand that they are part of this history,” he said. “So it’s very nice to share, and it’s also very nice to share in a context which is culturally different, and also difference is very important because difference allows you to understand aspects you never thought of.”

title: ‘A new house in town’: The $1 billion Powerhouse receives a joyous reception
text:
Advertisement

The Herald charts the ups and downs of the creation of Sydney’s newest cultural institution. See all stories .

After 11 years of planning, three years of construction, two parliamentary inquiries, four NSW premiers and a bill of $1 billion, Powerhouse Parramatta, the city’s newest cultural landmark, has opened to the public, with the NSW government declaring the museum Sydney’s answer to The Smithsonian and London’s British Museum. Long-running controversies over the project’s location, costs, focus and collection were set aside as the vertiginous Moreau Kusonski and Genton-designed building with its striking exoskeleton drew a wave of excitement and wonderment from a crush of curious visitors, just some of the 20,000 people who were expected to cross the threshold over its opening weekend. A dragon dance on the opening day. James Brickwood Without exception, visitors were taken aback by the ambition and spectacle of the marquee opening exhibition: Task Eternal, an exploration of space and flight in four chapters. Queues were longest in the museum’s only dedicated children’s show, The Dark, with its meteor tunnel, night forest and spaceship, for Es Devlin’s The Turning which has timed entry. The only slight grizzle at The Dark was that phones had to be placed out of sight in a sealed pouch to encourage sensory engagement.

Advertisement

Delighted children paddled bare-footed in the shallow pond of the Indigenous show, Overflow, while panoramic views from the CBD to the Blue Mountains through the soaring glass windows drew onlookers and selfies. Most visitors said they would be back. It was former premier Mike Baird who announced bombshell plans to relocate the Powerhouse in the state’s most populous region weeks out from the 2015 election. Premier Chris Minns and visiting schoolchildren from far western NSW cut the ribbon. Audrey Richardson Hours before opening, the Powerhouse Parramatta was ready for visitors. Audrey Richardson But it was Labor Premier Chris Minns who cut the ribbon on the monumental project – after a Coalition backflip on closure of its Ultimo home – with help from 18 visiting students of Menindee Central School, the museum’s first overnighting students.

Advertisement

Minns declared the museum “open for business” shortly after 10am, later admitting that Labor’s historic opposition to the project had been “wrong” and the museum would be “city shaping”. “I think it’s important that I acknowledge that at different points over the last few years, when we were in opposition, we were sceptical about this project. We wanted a cultural institution in western Sydney, but we did criticise this project. We were wrong. This is fantastic. This is going to be great for western Sydney. It’s going to be great for NSW.” Related Article Analysis

Development The face missing from the opening of the new Powerhouse Arts minister John Graham acknowledged the role of the museum’s absent chief executive – Lisa Havilah, who was stood down 72 days ago pending the outcome of a formal misconduct investigation – prompting cheers from members of the audience. Appointed in 2019 and a critical force in the building’s design, fitout and shows, Havilah was not invited to the event. “There’s an investigation taking place, and we need to make sure that’s done,” Minns later said. “But I think that you can do two things at the same time. You can pay tribute to the enormous work that Lisa and others have put into the institution while respecting the need for an independent investigation.”

Advertisement

Asked if the inquiry would be resolved quickly, Graham said: “One of the issues with that process is people have got a right to be able to contribute more material and ask for more time. We will not short-circuit that process.” The museum is staging five shows, all of which are free except for Task Eternal, where visitors aged over 16 pay $30. Accessing James Turrell’s Shangri La (Over the Hump) within that exhibition will cost an additional $10. The Roselands shopping centres. “raindrop fountain”, part of The Mall, one of the new museum’s exhibitions. Sam Mooy Visitors explore the exhibition. Audrey Richardson After weeks of prevarication, the museum’s open hours for exhibition shows from November 30 were confirmed as 10am to 5pm, with Friday late entry, a retreat on original plans to run the Powerhouse as a 24-hour museum, with nightly events, overnight stays and apartments for visiting artists and scientists.

Advertisement

The opening of 30 serviced apartments built on the top floor of the Powerhouse Parramatta and fitted out at a cost of more than $3 million has been delayed. These are to cater for visiting artists and scientists, but the logistics and management remains under review. Powerhouse says it has secured 18 contracted bookings for its commercial spaces, through to June 2027, from business, industry, cultural and government organisations. The announcement on the museum’s opening hours raises questions about the size of the workforce required now that the museum will be brought in line with all other cultural institutions. Visitors streamed into the new museum. James Brickwood Minns committed to funding the museum’s operations sufficiently to enable it to live up to its potential. “It’s not cheap, and it does cost taxpayer money, but we believe this is an investment in the future. The fixed costs of this beautiful building mean that you’ve got to have world-class exhibitions inside their halls.” Powerhouse Trust president David Borger lobbied for western Sydney’s first state significant cultural institution. “As a young bloke growing up in Parramatta I walked past this site … on my way to school. There was a car park here. It was the ugliest building on the Parramatta River, and never in my wildest dreams would I have thought that we’d actually have this magnificent cultural institution built. We haven’t done anything like this, frankly, since the Opera House. But there’s a new house in town.”

Advertisement

The unfurling of a banner declaring the Powerhouse “not a museum” and “vale Willow Grove” alluded to two of the many controversies which have embroiled the project – the demolition of historic building Willow Grove, which made way for the redevelopment, and ongoing controversy over its remit and treatment of its priceless collection. Long-time heritage advocate Suzette Meade said she was not surprised by the action given the street protests in 2021 and the extent of feeling. “Five years after the demolition of Willow Grove, the community’s blood still boils over this project. The NSW government underestimated the damage it caused, the disrespect it showed and how deeply it disenfranchised the people of Parramatta. We will never forget.” Protest banners reminding Sydney of the heritage building that was demolished to build the new museum in Parramatta. Audrey Richardson The day began with an official ribbon-cutting ceremony, kicked off by a Welcome to Country, with seven of the eight children who were present for the 2019 groundbreaking ceremony attending as young adults. The proceedings were watched by some of the museum’s youngest collaborators, Thoedore Bui, Jason Cilia and Tyler Pham Luu, all aged four, who donated toys to the museum’s dedicated children’s show, The Dark. Following the Australian Museum opening in 1827, major state arts spending had remained clustered east of Sydney Olympic Park, and this project marks a reshaping of Parramatta and a less CBD-centric arts scene.

Advertisement

For arts advocate John Kirkman, who was on the advisory committee that had lobbied for funding equity in western Sydney, the Powerhouse stands alongside the Sydney Opera House as an institutional project that is both controversial and transformative. Related Article Visual story

Development Inside Sydney’s newest billion-dollar house “I take a broader view on these massive cultural developments,” he says. “They are rare, transformative, and signal something profoundly positive about cultural production and public investment. A Sydney without the Opera House is inconceivable today – it delivered far more than anyone anticipated at the time. This is that same kind of moment.” For Kirkman, the investment holds generational weight. “Growing up in Granville, I lived in a fibro house with no books and no art, but I loved the idea of a museum,” he recalls. “I used to take the train to the Powerhouse at Ultimo and spend the day there. It was amazing because it was so far removed from my immediate world. This new institution has the power to open up the world to so many young people in that exact same way.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. Jokes radiate throughout Queensland’s cricket scene when it comes to Jem Ryan, though there would be few quips that are as flattering as what the blossoming paceman receives. Ryan is poised to lead the next generation of fast bowlers. AAPIMAGE “He sort of possesses [the Boland traits] – he bowls over perpendicular, he can move the ball and wing the ball both ways if he wants, but he just focuses on control, which is one of his strengths,” the Bulls bowling coach told this masthead. “He doesn’t try to get too fancy or too clever, he just repeats and repeats ball after ball, and it’s really impressive to watch. Bennett laughed that Ryan perhaps considered himself to be a budding AFL star before honing his focus on cricket, given his older brother Samson managed 31 games for the Richmond Tigers between 2021 and 2026. But the 22-year-old has pursued his ambition to become a future spearhead of the Baggy Green, as he leads a contingent of six Queensland quicks all aged 22 or under eager to announce themselves as potential successors to Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Pat Cummins. title: Australia's biggest cultural project since the Opera House goes live
text:
IN BRIEF NSW Premier Chris Minns and Arts Minister John Graham officially opened the Powerhouse Parramatta on Saturday.

An opening festival running over three weeks and four weekends will feature 179 events, most of which are free.

After almost 15 years, the doors of Australia's newest museum, Powerhouse Parramatta, are officially open to the public.

The billion-dollar museum has been described as the largest cultural infrastructure project in Australia since the Sydney Opera House.

About 3,000 objects are on display across 18,000 square metres of exhibition and public space, making it the state's largest museum. On its opening weekend, 25,000 visitors have registered to attend events.

The museum's interim CEO, Abbie Galvin, has said it's wonderful to see the project finally completed.

"It is now a building that is for the community of Western Sydney, the community of New South Wales and of course, Australia," she said. "It is an incredible cultural institution."

"And it represents innovation. It represents education. And it absolutely represents wonderment."

NSW Premier Chris Minns and Arts Minister John Graham opened the riverfront building on Saturday, saying it would be a magnet for Australians looking to spend time engaging with science and culture for free.

Some of the museum's exhibitions do, however, have an entry fee.

Powerhouse Parramatta's opening festival program will run until 29 November. Credit: Powerhouse Studios

Minns also credited former Coalition premier Mike Baird for beginning the project, telling reporters that his party had been wrongly critical of it when in opposition.

"We were wrong," Minns said. "This is fantastic. This is going to be great for Western Sydney. It’s going to be great for NSW," he said.

The opposition, too, was keen to highlight its contribution.

"Western Sydney has been waiting for its fair share and the Liberals and Nationals have delivered. If Labor had won the election in either 2015 or 2019, Powerhouse Parramatta would not be here today," it said in a joint statement.

Powerhouse Parramatta to become global destination

The striking building is covered in a lattice made of 1,300 individual pieces of steel and is the first public building in Australia awarded six green stars under the Green Building Council of Australia's new rating system.

It has a 24-hour accessible outdoor space with gardens, amphitheatres, and promenades linking the Parramatta River to Phillip Street.

An opening festival program over three weeks and four weekends will feature 179 different events, the majority of which are free, across First Nations' culture, science and technology, design, music, film and food.

Acclaimed British artist Es Devlin, whose works make up part of the opening exhibitions, has said she thinks the new museum will become a global destination.

Es Devlin's The Turning installation is one of Powerhouse Parramatta's opening exhibitions. Credit: Powerhouse Studios

"It's the first time that the building gets to sing," she told ABC Radio about the opening. "It's almost like the builders have been crafting this Stradivarius [violin] for seven years, and now is the first time it's given its voice and it meets its public."

"This one is really in a class of its own."

The Sydney Morning Herald has reported that the opening day of the Powerhouse Parramatta is "packed", with crowds and queues for each of the five opening exhibitions.

Attendees have described the building as "instantly iconic" and said that, despite the long wait and the political battles over it, the new Powerhouse appears to have been worth it.

Powerhouse Parramatta's predecessor, Powerhouse Ultimo, is undergoing a $300 million heritage restoration and rebuild project on its 1988 structure. While it too has been delayed by controversies and budget blowouts, it is anticipated to open in late 2028 or early 2029.

title: The grim news for Australian travellers quietly updated this week

Meanwhile, Westpac has said a surprising number of Australians are ahead on their mortgage repayments.

Australians could soon face higher airfares and fewer flights as Qantas responds to rising fuel costs. Meanwhile, shoppers hoping for big bargains as David Jones enters voluntary administration could be left disappointed.

And as interest rates rise again, new figures reveal just how far ahead some borrowers are on their repayments.

That means more expensive tickets for consumers, and fewer flights to choose from on certain routes. The cuts will be coming from its domestic operations.

However, it would appear that more recent price increases haven't deterred Qantas' customers, with the company saying demand remains resilient.

The carrier said international demand across its Qantas and Jetstar brands remains strong, with flyers redirecting travel away from the Middle East.

Of course, those international jaunts may give travellers something to think about, depending on their destination.

The Australian dollar lost around 2 per cent over the week, roughing up the exchange rate for certain popular holiday spots.

David Jones bargains uncertain

It's quite common for retailers entering voluntary administration to hold major sales and offload some excess inventory, but it might be a little different for David Jones — there could be less to sell.

This week, the iconic Australian department store called in a team to manage the business after it wound up in financial trouble.

However, as University of Technology retail expert Gary Mortimer told SBS' On the Money Podcast, David Jones operates a largely concession-based model under which brands retain control.

"They own that space, they own that inventory, they own that staff," Mortimer said.

READ MORE How David Jones could emerge from administration a very different retailer

"It's likely those brands will go in and collect that inventory whilst they can and move it to their physical store assets."

The administrators are now working through restructuring options, including the closure of some stores. That's where some bargains may ultimately be found.

"If it's a David Jones' branded product, you'd expect to see either some discounting or ideally maybe moving that inventory to stores that will be retained," Mortimer said.

David Jones is the world's oldest continuously running department store still operating under the same name.

Are you ahead on your repayments?

While the Reserve Bank's fifth interest-rate hike of the year will be painful for many, it would appear there are some borrowers who may be able to absorb that increase.

This week, Westpac revealed 37 per cent of its customers are more than two years ahead on their repayments.

In fact, 53 per cent have buffers of six months at the very least. Just 1 per cent of customers are behind.

title: Chris v Chris: What to know about New Zealand's tightly wedged election
text:
In Brief Chris Luxon and Chris Hipkins are locked in a tight race to lead New Zealand's next government.

Minor parties could hold the balance of power in an election expected to be too close to call.

Across the Tasman, New Zealanders are preparing to head to the polls in what is shaping up to be a tightly contested election.

It will be a battle of two Chrises.

In one corner is Christopher Luxon, the current prime minister and leader of the centre-right National Party, who is seeking a second term leading his coalition government.

In the other is Chris Hipkins, the leader of the centre-left Labour Party, who briefly served as prime minister after Jacinda Ardern resigned in 2023 before losing office later that year.

With campaigning now wrapped up, New Zealanders will vote on Saturday 7 November to decide who forms the country's next government.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Here's what you need to know.

Who are the two main players?

Chris Luxon, National Party

Luxon is New Zealand's current prime minister and has led the country since 2023.

The former Air New Zealand chief executive led the centre-right National Party back into government after defeating Labour three years ago.

New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon is hoping for a second term under his conservative coalition. Source: AAP / Ben Mckay

His campaign has focused heavily on the economy, including plans to return the budget to surplus and expand New Zealand's KiwiSaver retirement scheme.

But his first term has been turbulent. Luxon survived two confidence votes from National MPs this year amid weak polling, economic pressure and tensions within his governing coalition.

Chris Hipkins, Labour

Hipkins is seeking to return Labour to government three years after its election defeat.

The 48-year-old became prime minister in January 2023 following Jacinda Ardern's resignation, but served for less than a year before losing office at the October election.

Since then, he has campaigned on cost of living relief, stronger public services and investment in housing, infrastructure and healthcare.

Former New Zealand prime minister Chris Hipkins is hoping to get back into the top job after losing power in 2023. Source: AAP / Bianca De Marchi

How do New Zealand elections work?

New Zealand uses what's known as a mixed-member proportional (MMP) electoral system.

Voters cast two votes: one for their local electorate representative and one for the political party they want to govern.

People of Māori descent can choose whether to enrol on the general electoral roll or the Māori electoral roll.

Parliament is usually made up of 120 seats. Seventy-one are elected from geographic electorates, including seven Māori electorates, while the remainder are allocated according to each party's share of the nationwide vote.

A party generally needs at least 5 per cent of the party vote, or to win an electorate seat, to enter parliament.

Because seats are allocated proportionally, it is uncommon for a single party to win an outright majority.

That means coalition governments are the norm.

Every government since MMP was introduced in 1996 has relied on support from smaller parties, with the exception of Jacinda Ardern's Labour government in 2020.

Why the minor parties could decide the result

While much of the attention has focused on Luxon and Hipkins, smaller parties could ultimately determine who forms the next government.

Polling suggests neither National nor Labour is likely to win enough seats to govern alone, making coalition negotiations crucial.

These are the parties likely to play a major role:

New Zealand First: Led by veteran politician Winston Peters, the right-wing populist party is campaigning on issues including immigration, energy prices and withdrawing from the Paris climate agreement.

ACT : Led by deputy prime minister David Seymour, the libertarian-leaning party has focused on immigration, crime and reducing the size of government.

The Greens: Labour's most likely coalition partner, campaigning on climate action, tax reform and cost-of-living measures, including a proposed wealth tax.

Te Pāti Māori: Focused on Māori rights and representation, and expected to retain several Māori electorates.

Opportunity (TOP) : A centrist party led by Qiulae Wong that has never won a seat in parliament but is hovering around the 5 per cent threshold needed to enter parliament and could become a kingmaker.

What are the main issues for voters?

Like many countries around the world, the cost of living remains New Zealand's top election issue.

Inflation has eased from earlier highs, but households continue to face pressure from petrol prices, housing costs and everyday expenses.

The country's unemployment rate has risen to 5.7 per cent, its highest level in 11 years, while economic growth has remained sluggish following a prolonged downturn.

Healthcare has also emerged as a major campaign issue amid concerns about strained hospitals, staffing shortages and long waiting times for treatment.

Housing affordability remains a longstanding problem, particularly for younger New Zealanders trying to enter the property market.

Immigration, government spending, climate policy and Māori issues have also featured prominently throughout the campaign.

What's at stake on Indigenous issues?

The election comes after years of heated debate about Māori rights and representation, particularly around the Treaty of Waitangi, New Zealand's founding agreement between Māori leaders and the British Crown.

The coalition government has rolled back several policies designed to give Māori greater representation in public decision-making, while ACT has campaigned against what it calls "race-based" policies and has proposed abolishing the Waitangi Tribunal.

Meanwhile, Te Pāti Māori has sought to mobilise Indigenous voters and frame the election as a pivotal moment for Māori representation.

Because the overall contest is so close, the outcome in the seven Māori electorates could also influence coalition negotiations after election day.

What does the polling indicate?

Most polls suggest the race is too close to call.

The latest poll from Post-Freshwater Strategy, released on Friday, placed the opposition Labour Party slightly ahead, but still with no clear outcome for the election.

But it also placed the Opportunity Party at 5.1 per cent — just above the threshold for representation in parliament. If it crosses that line, it could emerge as a kingmaker in coalition talks.

Another October poll from Roy Morgan placed the centre-right bloc of National, ACT and NZ First as holding a narrow lead over Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori.

Another poll by Infrastructure New Zealand, an industry association, released on Friday, put Labour at 30.7 per cent and National at 26.4 per cent.

Analysts have also noted growing support for smaller parties, reflecting frustration among some voters with New Zealand's two major parties.

When is New Zealand's election and when will we know the results?

New Zealanders will head to the polls on Saturday 7 November, with voting closing at 7pm local time (5pm AEDT).

More than 1.4 million votes had already been cast during advance voting by the middle of election week.

Early results are expected to start emerging shortly after polls close, but New Zealand may not know who will form government on election night.

If no party wins enough seats to govern outright, major parties will need to negotiate coalition or support agreements with smaller parties, a process that can take days or even weeks.

That places the centrist Opportunity Party in a unique position. The party says it is willing to work with either side of politics and, if it enters parliament, could have significant influence over who forms New Zealand's next government.

What is clear, however, is that whichever major party wins the most votes is likely to need support from at least one smaller party, meaning coalition negotiations could ultimately decide who becomes New Zealand's next prime minister.

— With additional reporting by Australian Associated Press and Reuters.

title: How the US midterm results could 'cascade through' the AI and data centre industry
text:
In Brief Democratic candidates have been elected in several key states currently at the centre of data centre growth.

The results of this week's midterm elections have prompted significant drops in tech stocks internationally.

This week, voters in 13 US states were asked more than just who they wanted to represent them in Congress — they were also asked about a controversial new fixture in their neighbourhood: data centres.

According to analysis by Ballotpedia, at least 50 local ballot measures related to data centres.

The non-profit, which provides ballot information to voters around the country, tracked propositions put to voters across Arkansas, California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, North Dakota, Ohio and Wisconsin.

With three measures left to be decided later in the year, voters in the United States overwhelmingly rejected the development of data centres in their area.

All but one of the ballot measures failed.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The exception was in the small town of Harwood, North Dakota, where voters rejected an additional review of industrial projects, including data centres.

The largest proportion of motions were put to voters in Ohio, with 21 measures rejected across 18 jurisdictions.

It's one of several key states for data centre development, including Virginia, Texas, Georgia, California and Illinois.

Thousands of data centres have already been built across the US. Source: SBS News

Texas Democrat governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned to increase regulation and promised a moratorium on data centre construction. She is one of many pro-regulation candidates elected.

The trend has started to concern analysts, as shares in AI companies and tech-heavy stock indexes fell sharply on Thursday.

The US has far more data centres than any other country in the world following explosive growth in the past year.

The market reaction

The midterm results came as US stock markets had their worst day in 19 months amid fears of an AI slowdown as sellers shift stock that now carries risk.

Chipmaker Nvidia's shares dropped by at least 9 per cent, reducing its market value by US$400 billion ($580 billion). Shares in AMD and Micron, which also produce parts needed for AI computing, dropped more than 17 per cent.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq finished at least 5.5 per cent lower, according to Dow Jones data, while Japan's Nikkei 225 also fell as Asian chipmakers suffered.

Brad Conger, chief investment officer at investment firm Hirtle & Co, said the sell-off was the result of several factors, including concerns about ongoing financing and regulation of data centres.

"Some investors have reached the limit where they just have to liquidate risk entirely," he told Reuters.

Australia's markets largely avoided the global rout, with the ASX much more bank than tech-focused.

Chief investment officer at Opal Capital Management, Omkar Joshi, told SBS News' On the Money podcast the major falls in the US, Japan and South Korean exchanges are likely a symptom of reality setting in after overspend on AI, but he said it's not necessarily a case of the bubble popping.

"Funding costs have been blowing out for a while now, and it's really more just a reset of that reality rather than anything else that's coming through now.

"There was a lot of investor optimism in (the AI) space, and there wasn't always a lot of rationality on certain elements of the market."

He said the market reaction has created a "difficult" environment for Anthropic, which is preparing to launch the world's biggest public offering.

Trump has blamed the crash on the Democrats, only a day after celebrating what he called "another record high" for the stock market.

"The stock market suffered one of the worst days in history based on the results of the election," he said in a post on his Truth Social platform.

"Such a sad thing to watch! It took so much work to get us to a level that no one has ever seen before, and then this."

For some investors, it's been a clear sign of public sentiment.

"In our view, the significance of these midterm elections is more like a referendum on AI than a referendum on (Donald) Trump," Aidan Yao, a senior investment strategist at the Amundi Investment Institute, told Reuters.

What happens now?

Tapas Strickland, CEO of share trading platform Moomoo Australia, warned the governor's races in Texas and Georgia could significantly slow infrastructure rollout.

"Those two states effectively make up about a third of all AI data centre spend and projects," he told Reuters.

"If both of those go Democrat at the governor level, the potential for it to slow is very much there, and that would obviously cascade through to the rest of the AI sector."

Hinojosa and fellow Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms both won their seats with considerable margins. Bottoms and Amy Acton, governor-elect of Ohio, have also supported moratoriums on large data centre construction.

A slowdown in data-centre infrastructure could further impact not only the financial stability of operators, but also energy producers, chipmakers and cloud companies.

The impact could extend beyond the US, as operators look to more advantageous jurisdictions.

One potential result, according to analysts at HSBC, is that data centre operators move to more lenient states or countries should incoming leaders increase regulation.

title: More than three months after the World Cup, why haven't the Socceroos been paid?
text:
in brief Some Socceroos are still chasing Football Australia for 2026 FIFA World Cup pay.

The team has also petitioned have their match in Jordan moved due to the war in the Middle East.

Socceroos players who competed at this year's FIFA World Cup in North America are yet to be paid their match fees, three months after the tournament finished.

Just days after it was revealed that both male and female national team players were taking legal action against Football Australia (FA) over their revenue-sharing agreement, members of the 2026 Socceroos World Cup squad are pursuing Australia's football governing body for match payments.

Payment was due within a fortnight of the date they broke camp.

Australia were knocked out of the tournament at the round-of-32 stage in a loss to Egypt on 3 July.

FA, which recorded a $23 million loss over the last two financial years, said tax complications in the United States caused the delay.

The body said it was working with the players' union, Professional Footballers Australia (PFA), to "resolve the outstanding matters as quickly as possible" and that it was ready to make the payments.

"Before those payments can be processed, however, we require final specialist advice on the North American taxation obligations applicable to the payments, as well as some further player distribution information being provided through the PFA," FA said in a statement.

"Recognising the complexity of North American taxation requirements, FIFA facilitated access to specialist tax support for all participating member associations to help them understand and meet their respective obligations.

"We have been actively engaging with those specialist advisers since the World Cup to confirm the applicable tax and withholding treatment."

If a player sees game time, or is an unused substitute for the national team, they earn around $6,000 in match fees.

The Socceroos played two friendlies against Mexico and Switzerland before three World Cup group games and the Egypt shootout defeat, meaning players named for all six games are heading into camp this week out of pocket by roughly $36,000.

There were no known payment issues for the four friendlies which took place in the US in the October and November windows last year.

PFA chief executive Beau Busch said the situation was unacceptable.

"Any matter related to international tax was foreseeable and should have been addressed long before a ball was kicked at the tournament," he said.

Members of the squad who faced Brazil in two friendlies in Queensland in September are understood to have been paid in full.

Socceroos petition for Jordan match to move

FA's delay in paying World Cup match fees comes as players head into November's friendly window in the Middle East.

Some players have expressed concerns about travelling to the region — Australia will face Qatar in Doha and Jordan in Amman — amid the wider conflict.

The purpose of those friendlies in the current climate has been brought into question since the Asian Football Confederation opted to delay the Asian Cup.

Socceroos players, via their union, have urged FA to reschedule or relocate their upcoming friendly against Jordan in Amman due to safety concerns.

The Asian Football Confederation postponed that tournament, originally scheduled for January-February in Saudi Arabia, following the attack on Riyadh's international airport by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.

The Socceroos squad was expected to be named on Friday, but the announcement has been pushed back to the weekend amid uncertainty over whether some players will withdraw.

Indonesia's football association has already cancelled a 13 November planned friendly against Jordan in Amman amid an escalation in violence in the area, and the PFA made it clear Australian players didn't want to proceed.

"The PFA has worked with Football Australia over recent weeks in relation to security concerns regarding the upcoming assembly and engaged its own independent security experts," Busch said.

"With the full support of the PFA, the players have overwhelmingly expressed their view that the Jordan match should be rescheduled or relocated.

"We are committed to working with FA to reach a sensible solution."
