title: These Kiwis were driven to Australia by rising costs. Could an election bring them home?
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Despite working fewer hours and earning less, the Ririnui family has more money left over each week on the Gold Coast than they did in Auckland.

Tajai Ririnui, 32, her husband, and three daughters moved from New Zealand just three months ago after struggling to make ends meet amid a cost of living crisis that showed little sign of easing.

"After rent, fuel, kindy, groceries and putting money aside for things like power, water and internet, we were left with next to nothing," she tells SBS News.

"Don't get me wrong, we had everything we needed, but there was no room to save, no room for extra activities with our girls and very little opportunity to actually enjoy life.”

Ririnui's husband Jayden, 31, worked in floor restoration in New Zealand, putting in 12-hour days, sometimes six or seven days a week, to support the family. He now works as a scaffolder on the Gold Coast.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"We're averaging below what we were getting in New Zealand, but we have more left over, which is ironic because we're working less," Tajai says.

The pull home is very strong, but honestly, you'd rather … have everything and that little bit more here than be broke and have nothing at home.

Tajai Ririnui and her family moved to the Gold Coast due to the high cost of living in New Zealand. Source: Supplied

The Ririnuis are not alone.

Australia's higher wages and broader employment opportunities have long drawn New Zealanders across the Tasman, where they can live and work indefinitely under the Trans-Tasman Travel Arrangement. The movement has continued even as the economic gap between the two countries has fluctuated over time.

In the year to March 2026, an estimated 47,900 New Zealanders moved to Australia, while about 19,900 New Zealanders moved in the opposite direction, leaving a net migration loss of about 27,900 people, according to Stats NZ.

But beyond the headline migration figures, new research suggests more young New Zealanders are leaving for Australia and elsewhere overseas for the long term, raising concerns about the country's economic future.

As New Zealanders prepare to vote in Saturday's general election, the question is whether the next government can turn the tide and convince more of them to stay.

Why Kiwis are leaving

Former New Zealand prime minister Jacinda Ardern renewed attention on the country's emigration debate when she settled on Sydney's Northern Beaches earlier this year.

She joined the nearly 620,000 New Zealand-born people already living in Australia as of 2024 — representing about one in eight Kiwis.

Source: SBS News

The number of arrivals ebbs and flows depending on how each country's economy is performing. But a new report suggests more young people are making the move with little intention of returning.

About 77,500 New Zealanders aged 18 to 30 left the country long term for Australia and elsewhere between 2023 and 2025 — 60 per cent above the pre-pandemic average — according to Victor Consulting research commissioned by New Zealand's Green Party.

Of those who left, more than four in 10 are not expected to return, according to the research, potentially resulting in the permanent loss of NZ$12 billion ($9.7 billion) in education and healthcare investment.

Paul Spoonley, a New Zealand sociologist and emeritus professor at Massey University, says young New Zealanders have traditionally left in two groups: school leavers and graduates in their mid-20s.

He links the recent departures to graduates struggling to find work in New Zealand while Australian employers actively recruit, particularly in health and policing.

The Auckland skyline. The number of arrivals from New Zealand to Australia often depends on how each economy is performing. Source: Bloomberg / Becki Moss

Historically, around half of New Zealanders who moved to Australia eventually returned to New Zealand, but Spoonley suspects a larger share of the current wave may stay overseas.

"What we'd normally expect is that as the economic conditions in New Zealand improve over the medium to short, long term, then the migration would ease," he tells SBS News.

But I'm not sure that those economic conditions in New Zealand are going to be as short-term as we thought.

New Zealand has experienced a years-long economic downturn, with two recessions since 2022. Although the economy has begun to recover, unemployment remains elevated at 5.7 per cent, an 11-year high, compared with 4.7 per cent in Australia.

Last month, New Zealand finance minister Nicola Willis announced the National Party's election commitments to encourage young Kiwis to stay or return home. These include plans to legislate for lower student loan repayments, expand a 5 per cent home deposit scheme and extend paid parental leave, if the coalition government is returned to office.

But New Zealand economist Shamubeel Eaqub is sceptical there is an easy solution to stemming the flow of people overseas, pointing to four decades of faster wage growth in Australia.

Economist Shamubeel Eaqub says there are no easy solutions to entice New Zealanders to stay. Source: Supplied

In 2009, then prime minister John Key set a target of closing the income gap with Australia by 2025 — a goal that was never met.

"Obviously, we didn't, and so therein lies the issue. Politicians have learned from that a little bit, and they're less gung-ho about proclaiming they're going to somehow close the gap with Australia," Eaqub tells SBS News.

The cost of staying

Another New Zealander planning to make the move is Lisa Robb, 47, who has lived in Katikati, a town of 6,000 people roughly two hours' drive south-east of Auckland, with her family for 23 years.

After work dried up for her husband Manny's plastering business, he moved to Perth in February.

Lisa Robb (third from the left) is planning to join her husband, Manny (third from the right), in Perth after her youngest son finishes school. Source: Supplied

In New Zealand, he often worked seven days a week. In Perth, he now earns three times as much while working Monday to Friday, Robb says.

Two of her adult children have already moved to Australia in search of better opportunities, as have her stepson and his young family.

She plans to join them after her 15-year-old son finishes school.

"You just don't get to live a life because you're too busy working to make the money that you need just to survive, not even thrive, just survive," Robb tells SBS News.

"We wouldn't even have considered it if we didn't need to."

I love my country … I love the culture here, I love my trees and my birds, and all the rest of it, but if you can't afford to live then you can't afford to live.

While some inflationary pressures, including global energy and commodity price shocks, are beyond the government's control, Robb believes domestic policy could do more to ease the pressure on households.

"If they want people to stop leaving New Zealand, then they have to make New Zealand a more attractive place to live and at the moment, New Zealand isn't an attractive place to live," she says.

"I don't know what the answer is ... I just know that I live here, and I have to pay my bills, and I can't afford to do that because of how expensive things are."

While economic factors remain the biggest driver of emigration, Mark Berger, who runs relocation company NZ Relo, says families are often chasing something harder to measure.

Source: SBS News

"It's all about hope … it's someone thinking about their future and how they can apply it to better their family and their circumstances," he tells SBS News.

A knife-edge contest

Saturday's election is shaping up as a tight contest, with Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's National Party polling at 30 per cent and the opposition Labour Party, led by former prime minister Chris Hipkins, on 29 per cent, according to the latest 1News Verian poll.

Government coalition parties ACT New Zealand and New Zealand First polled 10 per cent and 8 per cent respectively, leaving the right-wing bloc with a projected 58 seats — three short of the 61 needed for a majority in New Zealand's 120-seat parliament.

National Party leader Christopher Luxon (centre) has promised to cut government spending if re-elected. Source: Getty / Hagen Hopkins

The left-wing bloc, comprising Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori (the Māori Party), would secure 56 or 60 seats, depending on the outcome of the Māori electorate contests and potential parliamentary overhangs.

The poll also puts the Opportunity Party on 6 per cent, potentially giving it seven MPs and a significant say in post-election coalition negotiations. Neither major bloc is projected to secure a majority on its own.

The election is being fought against a backdrop of mounting pressure on household budgets.

An Ipsos poll released last week found 64 per cent of respondents believed the cost of living was the country's biggest issue, followed by healthcare at 45 per cent, fuel prices (31 per cent), the economy (30 per cent) and unemployment (19 per cent).

While inflation has eased from its post-pandemic peak, it remained at 3.7 per cent in the 12 months to September, above the Reserve Bank's target range of 1 to 3 per cent. Although down from 4.1 per cent in the year to June, many households have yet to experience sustained relief.

National's approach to tackling the cost of living centres on cutting government spending — including reducing the public service workforce by nearly 9,000 – and delivering tax relief.

Labour, meanwhile, has pledged to reduce household bills through free GP visits, capped public transport fares, a freeze on fuel taxes, and greater supermarket regulation. Its proposed capital gains tax on investment and commercial property would help fund its healthcare commitments.

Opposition leader Chris Hipkins' Labour Party is polling neck-and-neck with the National-led government. Source: Bloomberg / Brendon O'Hagan

Although frustrated with the pace of progress under National, Robb says she is leaning towards voting for either National or ACT New Zealand.

To be quite honest, I'd like a change, but that's really not going to make much difference.

"I like the way National is going; I just wish they'd get there a little bit faster. I think a lot of the problems that we have are COVID hang-ups, which really you can't blame on the government 100 per cent."

Tajai Ririnui, meanwhile, is hoping Labour will take office, believing a change of government could bring relief to middle-and lower-income families.

As a Māori woman, she sees the current National-led government's policy changes affecting Māori as another setback. She would like to see Te Pāti Māori in government but considers that unlikely.

"Our government seems determined to undermine Māori culture, and honestly, the state of things back home is heartbreaking," she says.

We are a minority, unfortunately, in New Zealand … we get treated as kind of like outsiders in our own country.

Since taking power in 2023, the National-led government has abolished the independent Māori Health Authority (Te Aka Whai Ora), prioritised English in official communications and backed the Treaty Principles Bill, which sought to redefine aspects of how the Treaty of Waitangi is interpreted. The bill was defeated at its second reading in April 2025.

Thousands protested in 2024 when the junior coalition party ACT New Zealand proposed legislation to redefine the founding treaty between Māori and the Crown. Source: Bloomberg / Mark Coote

The government has defended its approach as promoting equal treatment and common understanding of public services and the law.

New Zealand's Electoral Commission says about 126,000 enrolled voters have told it they are living overseas — up from 92,600 in 2023 — with the majority in Australia.

Spoonley says the growing number of overseas voters could be significant, given the traditionally younger demographic of New Zealanders living abroad and their potential influence on the election result.

"We've got people who've left New Zealand in the last two years ... who I suspect are quite disgruntled with some of the policy settings, and want to know that they're going to get a government that is more sympathetic.”

Would they ever return?

While Robb is a proud New Zealander, she struggles to see herself returning to New Zealand anytime soon once she's established a life in Australia.

"Everybody I know that's left New Zealand is loyal to New Zealand and wouldn't have left if they didn't have to," she says.

Lisa Robb says doesn't expect to return to New Zealand until she retires. Source: Supplied

"I will work out the rest of my working years in Australia," Robb says.

I don't want to die [in Australia], but New Zealand has to drastically change before I would consider coming back here, and I don't see that happening before I retire.

Ririnui, however, says the plan is to return home

"We moved to Australia for the money, and that's it. Our goal is to put our heads down, work hard and save as much as we possibly can over the next five, 10 years, with the hope of eventually returning home.

"Being Māori, we're spiritually and wholeheartedly connected to our whenua [land] and our whānau [extended family]. And even though we've only been away for a short time, we can feel that something is missing from our lives. Even our girls feel it."

title: The Bollywood connection you never expected to find in Alice Springs
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

"Welcome to paradise" were the first words Nishant Mahendru heard as he stepped out of Alice Springs Airport.

He thought it was a joke.

"I was trying to look for danger, like what's going to happen? Is someone going to throw something?" he tells SBS News.

He had come to the Red Centre of the Northern Territory for a two-week holiday. What happened next wasn't quite part of the plan. Mahendru, better known as Nish to those in Alice Springs, was born in the Punjab region of northern India. Against his parents' wishes, he left his small town after school to pursue hairdressing.

"In India, hairdressers don't get paid well, or they don't even get treated well. And I just said, 'I want to go to Mumbai because I'm going to work with Bollywood,'" Mahendru says.

And so he did. An opportunity to learn the craft through L'Oreal Paris in Mumbai opened the door to a dream first job at a celebrity salon.

Nishant Mahendru was featured in the Bombay Times in 2009 for cutting cricketer Ishant Sharma's hair. Source: Supplied

Soon after, Mahendru was rubbing shoulders with Bollywood actors Sunny and Bobby Deol, both prominent names in India's film industry, as well as Indian cricket stars including Sachin Tendulkar, Virat Kohli and Ishant Sharma.

Bollywood to Alice Springs

After working around the world and on a political campaign across India, Mahendru was exhausted.

"I was travelling overseas, staying in five-star hotels, flying in chartered planes and all this, living a very fancy life. But then I got bored. I was like, what's next for me?" he says.

He looked to Australia and was granted a Skilled Regional visa (subclass 489) in 2019.

"Sometimes I just get blessed. I got it in August 2019. In October, they announced that the visa is closed. No-one can apply for the visa anymore."

The "spiritual energy and welcoming community" of Alice Springs led Mahendru to fall in love with the town. He soon stumbled upon an opportunity to take over the lease of a local hair salon.

After borrowing money from friends, he made it happen.

"Deep down somewhere in my mind and heart, I did want to have my salon one day, but I didn't know how to do that. But this place made it happen so organically that now I think I can open 10 more salons," Mahendru says.

And so, Why Not by Nish was born. The salon's name is inspired by the 38-year-old's happy-go-lucky attitude.

For long-time Alice Springs resident Sarah North, Mahendru's salon represents the kind of community connection that makes the town special.

"It's up to each of us to sing loud from a song sheet that's really positive," she tells SBS News.

Alice Springs resident Sarah North encouraged Nishant Mahendru to open his own salon. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

The 69-year-old encouraged Mahendru to buy the salon, which she now visits regularly.

I'm very grateful for the Indian contribution to this town. I think it's added enormously a depth that Alice didn't have before.

Local music from Arrernte artists — the Traditional Custodians and First Nations owners of Mparntwe (the Alice Springs area) and the surrounding Central Australian region — often reverberates through the salon, helping it build a reputation as an inclusive space for Indigenous clients.

Nishant Mahendru visits the remote Northern Territory community of Kintore each year to provide free haircuts. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

"I think Nish has got quite a following in this town. Usually when I come here, there's stacks of people here that I know," North says.

Diwali in the Red Centre

For Mahendru, the journey from India has not meant leaving behind the traditions and memories that shaped him. As Diwali approaches, those connections take on renewed significance.

Widely known as the festival of lights, Diwali is one of the most significant celebrations for Hindus, Sikhs and Jains. Its significance and customs vary between communities, but the festival is broadly associated with the triumph of light over darkness and good over evil.

Celebrations commonly involve lighting traditional oil lamps, known as diyas, decorating homes, sharing food and gathering with family. For Mahendru, food plays a central role in his family's celebrations, involving days of planning to have a wide variety of meat and vegetarian dishes.

"More desserts and family getting together. All the family sitting in one house … [We] would play cards. It was a ritual one week before Diwali and one week after Diwali."

But growing up in a relatively poor area, Mahendru remembers a child next door who had "nothing" during a Diwali celebration in his youth.

Not even new clothes, not even thongs or shoes on his feet. That changed me as a person. I still have that memory. I can [still] see his eyes.

Mahendru says he shared fireworks with the boy — a memory that has forever changed how he sees the annual celebration.

"I don't need any fireworks. I don't need new clothes. I'm good."

For him, the memory reminds him that the festival's spirit is about more than material celebrations.

Across Alice Springs, many local businesses and community organisations are also preparing to mark Diwali, with food and festivities offering opportunities to bring people together.

At Indian Chef Restaurant, co-owner George Jacob has been preparing to sell new sweets for the celebrations. The town's Indian community includes people from different parts of the Indian subcontinent, bringing with them a diversity of regional cuisines and cultural traditions.

"We go [to] other groups and we celebrate and have very good friendship and relationship and a good harmony in Alice Springs," Jacob told SBS News.

George Jacob and his brother moved to Alice Springs in 2012 before opening two hospitality businesses. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

Meanwhile, the gurdwara (a Sikh place of worship) will open its doors for food and celebrations, with families gathering to pass on traditions to younger generations.

"We have a free kitchen, a communal kitchen on that day. Everybody can eat and enjoy. And even at home as well, we lit candles and praised God."

A world in Alice Springs

Alice Springs' multicultural population reflects a growing diversity across the Red Centre, with migrants from dozens of cultural backgrounds making the region home.

Analysis by the Multicultural Community Services of Central Australia (MCSCA) estimates first-generation migrants from 72 cultural groups now account for about one-third of the region's population.

MCSCA acting manager Joy Taylor says the Indian diaspora alone makes up an estimated 20 to 25 per cent of the migrant population.

"We're looking at this area that's three times the size of Victoria. So, the impact of increasing numbers of migrants is much more significant than in other parts of the country," she tells SBS News.

It's the heartbeat of the world. It's the centre of our country.

For Jashan Singh, the connection to Alice Springs goes back much further.

His family moved to the town when he was 13, and after spending time interstate, the now 35-year-old has returned to help run the family car rental business.

His father and uncle established the business and chose an independent approach rather than operating under a franchise.

Jashan Singh splits his time between Alice Springs and Hobart, managing his family's car rental business. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

"It was my dad and my uncle, two brothers. They said, 'Why not? We can just try to do it ourselves. We don't need to try and get a franchise,'" Singh tells SBS News.

He says regional communities can offer opportunities for people willing to make a start.

Alice Springs has a lot to offer and it's much more than just a headline.

"There's certainly a lot of value in that where people are able to be themselves fully and without fear or without feeling rejected for who they are."

Nishant Mahendru and partner Brooke O'Connell recently welcomed a baby boy named Sunny. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

For Mahendru too, Alice Springs has become an unexpected place to call home — one where he has been able to pursue a career on his own terms, despite the doubts his family once had about his future.

"My mother was always stressed and anxious about it, [saying] that I'm not going to get anywhere in life because I'm not good at studies.

Now they are proud of me.

title: A month after Australia's card surcharge ban, here's what's happened to prices
text:
In Brief Coffee prices have increased over the last six months, with the average small flat white priced at $5.17.

When the Reserve Bank introduced a rule banning card surcharges, some were concerned it would push prices further.

At an average of $5.17, buying a small flat white will cost you more this month in some Australian cafes.

In April, the average small flat white cost $5.01. Five months later, before a controversial rule from the Reserve Bank went into effect, the average in September was $5.11.

While coffee prices have continued to rise over the last six months, the ban on businesses charging customers for card payments has many wondering whether the cost will be absorbed or added to the menu.

So, did cafes raise their prices?

One analysis found one in five cafes increased their prices in October, though the changes were not necessarily driven by the card surcharge ban alone.

That data comes from self-confessed coffee, data and automation nerd Chris Drake, the creator of Small Flat White, a website that has become an unofficial tracker of coffee prices across Australia

"I'm a real weird coffee person," he told SBS.

"I buy a pack of beans, and I'll use it at home and go to the cafe and see what it's meant to taste like, and I track every single piece of like coffee I have."

Drake started calling around coffee shops to find out which beans they offered, before realising it was a chance to ask other things too. He now tracks prices at thousands of cafes.

It's become the Small Flat White Price Index.

How much did prices go up?

The tracker only records how much prices change, not the factors that contribute to the rise or fall. But Drake said cafe owners tell him, anecdotally, that they are delaying raising prices for as long as possible and then planning to raise prices once.

Some 70 per cent of cafes charge a round price for their coffee. So, when raising their price, it is often changed to the next 50c increment or whole dollar.

An increase of 50 cents is typically about 10 per cent of the coffee price.

"But that's not because they're necessarily putting it up because of the surcharge; it's all the other costs too, and then they're putting it up 50 cents," he said.

READ MORE Card surcharges are banned. Now Aussies are fuming over another charge

"Cafe owners tell us their costs keep rising. They've got wages, super, rent, milk, beans, freight, even the cost of coffee cups."

Nearly 40 per cent of increases were 50 cents, with 20 cents the next most popular at 13 per cent. Nine per cent of increases were of 30 cents or a dollar.

Which states are paying the most?

ACT had the largest increase over the last six months at 4.2 per cent, closely followed by Queensland, NSW and Victoria with a 4 per cent increase since April.

Prices in South Australia have increased by 3 per cent. For Tasmania and Western Australia, it's only increased by 2.3 and 2.1, respectively.

Small Flat White also breaks down coffee prices by suburb.

READ MORE Everything you need to know about Australia's card surcharge ban

The suburbs currently offering the cheapest prices are in Sydney's south-west, with the average in Canterbury at $4.67 and Botany at $4.68.

The most expensive cups are being sold in north Queensland and South Australia's Yorke Peninsula. Prices tended to be higher in rural locations, with transportation costs also becoming more expensive.

What about other businesses?

Analysis from online payment company Tyro found nearly 90 per cent of businesses that previously charged card surcharges haven't raised their prices.

Twelve per cent of businesses previously using surcharges raised their prices during October, as did 2.7 per cent of businesses that never surcharged.

As for how much their prices went up, more than half of the increases were by more than three times the amount previously surcharged.

title: How David Jones could emerge from administration a very different retailer
text:
IN BRIEF David Jones will have to significantly "reduce its footprint" and invest in online shopping to keep doors open.

The retailer announced it has entered voluntary administration on Thursday after failed rental negotiations.

David Jones has been a giant on the Australian retail landscape for almost two centuries. But experts warn the retailer won't survive administration if it fails to "shrink and specialise".

Some have suggested it will look to US department stores for a model on downsizing and creating a David Jones 2.0.

The high-end chain announced it has entered voluntary administration on Thursday, after a failure to reach agreement with the retailer's main landlord over rent payments.

Some storefronts are expected to close, but David Jones will continue trading while administrators review its operations.

Danny Samson, chair of management at the University of Melbourne Business School's Department of Management, said the administration announcement was a "long time coming".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"They've had a department store business model in place for 180-plus years, which is a really long time for any company," he told SBS News.

"They haven't changed, but the world has moved on."

He said it's become common for department stores globally to lose market share and shrink.

Business strategist and consumer behaviour analyst Barry Urquhart told SBS News the retailer was suffering from "undercapitalisation".

"It doesn't have sufficient funds to be able to develop a business development program," he said.

"Therefore, when you run out of capital, you run out of time, and when you run out of time, your creditors run you out of business."

Urquhart warned the "cost of doing business" is now "profound and widespread".

"Margins have been squeezed. Consumers are entrenched value shoppers. They are price sensitive, they're informed, discerning, and very demanding."

He said consumers are becoming "less loyal" and are seeking "value and price" — it's making them turn to e-commerce.

More than 20 per cent of David Jones' revenue came from online purchases, according to retail marketing and consumer behaviour professor at the Queensland University of Technology, Gary Mortimer.

"It just goes to show you don't need so many physical stores if you can facilitate those online purchases elsewhere," he said.

"We've seen brands themselves become retailers too — brands you once went into a department store to access because you couldn't get them elsewhere now have their own physical retail stores."

Mortimer said the rise of "fast fashion" is also contributing to the department store's downfall.

The type of people spending has also shifted.

Samson said David Jones' business model has preferenced older people who have "less disposable income" than their younger counterparts.

"The big challenge for David Jones is how does it shed its old grand image for something that's new, nifty and cool and really appeals to the younger person with disposable income?"

'Something can be salvaged'

Not all hope is lost for the Australian icon, started by a Welshman named David Jones.

"There is possibly something that can be salvaged in the way of a smaller and sharper set of operations," said Samson.

He said David Jones' reputation means that with the right changes, the retailer can survive.

"They'll have to substantially change, and that includes shrinking, specialising and going where consumers want them to go," he said.

"David Jones will have to change its footprint substantially and reduce its overhead costs ... It'll have to have a new business model and be in a very different form, much more online presence, much more change in its product line."

Mortimer also believes the world's oldest department store still trading under its original name (it first started trading in 1838) will live on but he said it'll have to limit stores and rely on its luxury appeal.

"We will see David Jones 2.0," he said.

"It will be a smaller fleet of businesses. It will hark back to its days of champagne bars, luxury retail and luxury brands that you can't get in Australia."

He said David Jones may take a similar path to Saks Fifth Avenue in the United States, which went into voluntary administration at the start of 2026.

"By July this year, Saks came out of that process with only 15 stores, reducing their fleet from 33 stores — that's essentially what we'll see with David Jones," he said.

The news of David Jones' administration has raised concerns for Myer — which has already closed seven stores since 2019, and recently announced the closure of its Roselands store in Sydney.

"We'll continue to see a decline and a resize of the department store sector," Mortimer said.

title: Usman Khawaja remained silent for eight years. Why did he speak out now?
text:
Advertisement

SportCricketTest cricket Opinion Usman Khawaja remained silent for eight years. Why did he speak out now? Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist November 7, 2026 — 4:09pm

November 7, 2026 — 4:09pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australian cricket has itself to blame for the eight-year suppurating wound that has been reopened by Usman Khawaja’s memories of the South African tour of 2018. It bled in 2021 when Cameron Bancroft gave the interview that sealed his fate as an Australian representative. Former Test batsman Usman Khawaja has opened old wounds with his recollections of what occured in Cape Town, South Africa, in 2018. Dan Peled David Warner and his manager periodically reopened it. Left unhealed, it was always ready for a new bleed. If they’re looking for their beloved “learnings”, Cricket Australia, and Australia’s Test players, might look back to their failure in 2018 to honestly and broadly tell the truth about what happened at Newlands and on that tour.

Advertisement

Their window of opportunity for truth-telling lasted about a day, when they could have accepted collective responsibility and tried to bring the rest of the cricket world with them. Instead, they attempted to ring-fence the blame around Bancroft, Warner and Steve Smith, to punish those players and hope the heaviness of those punishments would be a substitute for treating the wound. As any battlefield surgeon could have told them, all they were doing was creating the conditions for a long-term recurrent infection. Their missteps started, but never finished, with that oldest of cricketing and human motives: looking after number one. Khawaja is right when he says his three teammates were scapegoats for a responsibility that should have been shared.

Advertisement

Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket ‘It was all of us’: Khawaja blows the whistle on more sandpaper use in South Africa in 2018 Did the bowlers know Bancroft took a specific piece of sandpaper onto the field at a specific time? No; we can take them at their repeated word. But they have not answered the question they are being asked, which is whether they knew, more broadly, that their team was altering the ball, as many other teams had done for decades, to enable reverse swing. The plausible deniability scheme – ask no questions, hear no lies – doesn’t wash. It didn’t wash for Smith, who as captain said he didn’t want to know the specifics. He paid the price for his dereliction of leadership. But it didn’t wash for the team, either.

Advertisement

Thanks to reverse swing, they won matches and series as a team, they reaped rewards as a team, they built a reputation as a team. Yet when the crunch came, Bancroft and Warner were isolated as individuals and only Smith was made to take wider responsibility. Why didn’t Khawaja speak earlier? His explanation, that he wasn’t asked, is only a partial defence. Cameron Bancroft was the most junior of the banned trio. Artwork: Maria Ercegovac He had every opportunity to reveal what he knew, behind closed doors, to Cricket Australia, and he chose not to. He, like everyone else, was looking out for number one. The only person who failed to look out for number one was Bancroft, through his naivete, implying in 2021 that the bowlers knew about the ball-tampering. He never played for Australia again.

Advertisement

The behaviour and treatment of Warner repeated it again and again. Look after number one because the collective won’t have the guts to step forward. Khawaja is accused of making his revelations now so that he can profit by selling books. Then newly sacked Australian cricket captain Steve Smith addresses the media at Sydney Airport in 2018, after arriving back from the ball-tampering scandal in South Africa. Janie Barrett Anyone who knows the first thing about books is laughing into their teacups. Khawaja has received his advance, he was well paid as a cricketer, and books aren’t that profitable. (Ask Warner, who prefers to protect his ongoing lucrative employment than throw it all away for the pyrrhic satisfaction of “selling books”.) Khawaja remained silent for eight years for the same reason everyone else did: it wasn’t in their personal interest. Now he wants to get it off his chest. It’s a bit late but it’s also about time someone was open with their version of the truth.

Advertisement

The fact that he’s waited for post-career, when he has less to lose, underscores the centrality of self-interest. Newlands offered a rare opportunity for Australian and international cricket. Ball-tampering, both contemporary and historic, could have been admitted and acknowledged. There was a chance for truth-telling and cleansing. This isn’t hindsight speaking. Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith face the media in Cape Town 2018. Getty Images On the day the scandal broke, many of us idealists pleaded for cricketers collectively to show a moral courage akin to the physical and mental courage they displayed on the field. It turns out that this would have been Khawaja’s preference, too. But instead of saying “me too”, past and present players united under a different response: me first. And here’s where it ends up. Damage reopened, friendships rebroken, families re-traumatised, cricket re-vandalised. It didn’t need to be this way but Cricket Australia and its players set the tone on day one.

Advertisement

If you’re not going to cauterise this wound, get set for a long, slow bleed. Improbably, it still isn’t too late. Khawaja has been brave, if belatedly. The members of that team and their staff need only admit that they consented, implicitly if not explicitly, to dirty tricks because they thought such tricks were endemic in Test cricket. That’s all Khawaja has done and all he is calling for: a bit of team spirit. Fat chance?

Advertisement

Maybe nothing has changed since Darren Lehmann’s first press conference as coach of an Australian team shamed by losing games. What was his responsibility? “To win,” he said, with one of those smiles that hinted that if you don’t understand it’s about winning, you don’t understand anything. It turned out that there was a bigger shame than losing, a shame with a long life that still has years to run. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday. title: Kevin Morby on being half of alt-country’s power couple
text:
“Now that I’m a bit older, I understand that time doesn’t have to be an enemy,” says Kevin Morby.

The singer-songwriter – who just welcomed a baby with his partner, Waxahatchee’s Katie Crutchfield – embraces change on his new album, Little Wide Open.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

There’s a new kid in town at Kevin Morby’s house. He hasn’t been there long, but he has changed the lives of the 38-year-old and his partner of almost a decade, fellow singer-songwriter Katie Crutchfield, who makes music as Waxahatchee. The two became parents to a baby boy three weeks before this interview, and everyone is asking Morby how he’s handling the lack of sleep. “And I have to tell them that we’re actually all sleeping fine,” says Morby. “The baby is really chill, but I feel weird about telling people that. I have a couple of other friends who just had children this year as well, and they aren’t getting much sleep, and I feel like they don’t want to talk to me. They kind of hate me.” Morby is speaking from the family’s mid-century ranch house in Kansas City – the couple divide their time between there and Los Angeles – ahead of an Australian tour behind his latest album, Little Wide Open. He wrote the songs when he and Crutchfield were contemplating their future, and he was aware his life was about to change. It made him think about time and his relation to it. “On my previous album, This Is a Photograph, which I love, it felt like being in a boxing ring with time, waiting to be knocked out. But now that I’m a bit older and making some big life decisions, I understand that time doesn’t have to be an enemy. It can be your companion if you’re on this trip together with someone.” Morby’s journey to this moment has had some definite turning points. He had a transient childhood, moving house multiple times due to his father’s job with General Motors. He was born in Lubbock, Texas, then the family shifted to Detroit, then Tulsa, then Oklahoma City, before settling in the suburbs of Kansas City. As a teenager, he suffered panic attacks.

Advertisement

“There were a couple of years in high school of just living moment to moment, terrified of when the next attack was going to happen. I eventually dealt with them through meds at first, and then a really good therapist, and I started eating more healthily and riding a bike all the time, which helped.” He also started playing music and joined a band, but it was when he played his first solo show at a bookstore that he had an epiphany, “because I couldn’t believe how cathartic it was. It was like finding this enlightenment, and it felt like a huge weight off my chest. It was exhilarating.” Morby with Katie Crutchfield of Waxahatchee, his partner of almost a decade. The couple welcomed their first child in July. Getty Images for The Recording Academy Soon afterwards, at the age of 17, he dropped out of high school, and after saving $600 from a job in an Indian restaurant, he got on an Amtrak train and moved to New York with a suitcase, a sleeping bag, his guitar and a four-track tape machine. He lucked out by scoring free board at a home in Brooklyn’s Carroll Gardens in exchange for babysitting. It was 2006, and he immersed himself in the vibrant music scene that was blossoming in Brooklyn at the time, seeing Jeffrey Lewis, Kimya Dawson, Dirty Projectors, TV on the Radio and more. Morby and Crutchfield had a meet-cute in 2012 while both playing on the same bill – at the merch table she undercut him on the price of a tour t-shirt to a prospective customer. They kept crossing paths on tour over the years and became friends, eventually getting together in 2017. Fans love dissecting their songs to decode whether they are writing about each other, none more so than the 2024 Waxahatchee breakout track, Right Back To It, an affecting ballad about keeping a long-term relationship alive, where Crutchfield duets with MJ Lenderman.

Advertisement

“I actually listened to it again yesterday when it came up randomly on a playlist and thought ‘Goddamn that’s a great song!’” says Morby. “There’s certainly a back and forth between us, where it feels like some of the songs are talking to each other. On this new album, I’ve been jokingly saying that I made it more Americana so Katie can really hear it and get into it.” In a recent interview, Crutchfield said, “it’s a strange situation to fall in love with an album that’s also kind of about your life.” The new song Bible Belt was inspired by a tragedy. A couple were on their way to see Morby play in Denver in 2021; they never made it. Their car was involved in a crash – the girl was badly injured and spent a long time in hospital; her boyfriend died. When Morby heard what had happened, he made contact with her. “I wrote Bible Belt in the back of the tour bus after hearing that news,” he says. “A year later, I’m in Paris and playing the Bataclan, where the horrible shooting happened in 2015. And I look down from the stage and there in the front row is this girl and she’s with her boyfriend’s mother. They said it was important for them to be there. Like a symbol, you know? “Touring can be a slog. You’re travelling a lot and trying to figure out where to eat and where to take a shit and you’re tired all the time. But then there are moments like that, when you realise there are people who have gone through hard times or tragedies, and in some small way you’ve helped them through. And that’s an honour.”

Advertisement

Sometimes the honour goes the other way. In 2016, Morby released a stand-alone protest song called Beautiful Strangers. It referenced Bataclan, along with the Pulse nightclub mass shooting in Orlando, Florida, and Freddie Gray, who died while in police custody in Baltimore in 2015. It’s a song about remembrance, solidarity and strength in the face of prejudice, brutality and violence. Years later he got a call telling him that the legendary gospel and soul singer Mavis Staples wanted to cover the song. It ended up on her most recent album, Sad and Beautiful World, and won the 86-year-old a Grammy for Best American Roots Performance. “I mean, this is someone Bob Dylan idolised,” he says. “She marched with Martin Luther King. She’s a historical figure. Everything she’s done in her life is just unbelievable. And here she is covering my song. “When we finally met, it was like being in the presence of greatness. And she said, ‘Kevin, you went to the other side of the mountain, and you wrote Beautiful Strangers, and you came back and gave it to all of us.’” He shakes his head. “It’s the most amazing thing that’s ever happened to me... Besides Katie and my son, of course,” he quickly adds, smiling. Kevin Morby’s Little Wide Open is out now. He will perform at Eltham’s The Eltham on November 12, Bellingen Golf Club on November 13, Brisbane’s Old Museum on November 14, Mt Glorious’ Elm House on November 15, Sydney’s Metro Theatre on November 18, Brunswick Heads’ Hotel Brunswick on November 20, Castlemaine’s Town Folk Festival on November 21, and Melbourne’s Forum on November 22.

With his clerical collar, black blazer and sunglasses, Monsignor Alberto Rocca cuts an imposing figure as he walks past the stark white of the Powerhouse Parramatta’s steel exoskeleton. And he should. Rocca holds a lot of power: he’s the gatekeeper of the Codex Atlanticus, a collection of 1119 pages from Leonardo da Vinci’s notebooks dating from 1478 to 1519, and the man responsible for delivering a small selection of the artist’s drawings from Milan to western Sydney. Monsignor Alberto Rocco at the Powerhouse Parramatta on opening day. Audrey Richardson Standing in the dimly lit room that houses the drawings, Rocca explained just what it takes to move the pages – which are so delicate, each page can only be displayed for three months at a time – safely to the other side of the world. “When you transfer important masterpieces you have a codified method, which is international,” he said.

Advertisement

The works are sealed in Milan in clima frames, a specialised, protective framing system that controls humidity, before they are placed in special crates to help keep the temperature low while they are on a plane. When the drawings arrived in Parramatta, Rocca said they were placed in showcases that have technology to allow for the temperature and light to continue to be controlled. “Light is very dangerous for drawings,” he said. “If you have some paper in your house and you put it under the sun for two days, it fades.” Monsignor Alberto Rocco stands in front of where the da Vinci drawings are displayed. Audrey Richardson While he’s explaining the importance of protecting the drawings from light, a news crew with a camera light on walks in, illuminating the dark room. He stops speaking and frowns, saying “this is very bad”. He looks relieved when they leave. The papers are part of Task Eternal, the museum’s flagship exhibition that unpacks humanity’s fascination with stars, flight and space. The da Vinci drawings of flying machines were transferred from Veneranda Biblioteca Ambrosiana – an institution that’s more than 400 years old. Rocca is director of the library’s art gallery.

Advertisement

Related Article City life Visitor’s guide to the new Powerhouse Parramatta It’s a strong contrast to the newly opened Powerhouse Parramatta, which the Catholic priest praises for its design and large exhibition space. Although he’s been to Sydney before, it’s his first time visiting Parramatta, and he said it was a nice feeling to see the drawings on display in a new environment. “When we have da Vinci and we have great masterpieces, they are world patrimony, and so for us to be here, it is also a way to share and to make also people in Parramatta to understand that they are part of this history,” he said. “So it’s very nice to share, and it’s also very nice to share in a context which is culturally different, and also difference is very important because difference allows you to understand aspects you never thought of.”

title: ‘A new house in town’: The $1 billion Powerhouse receives a joyous reception
text:
Advertisement

The Herald charts the ups and downs of the creation of Sydney’s newest cultural institution. See all stories .

After 11 years of planning, three years of construction, two parliamentary inquiries, four NSW premiers and a bill of $1 billion, Powerhouse Parramatta, the city’s newest cultural landmark, has opened to the public, with the NSW government declaring the museum Sydney’s answer to The Smithsonian and London’s British Museum. Long-running controversies over the project’s location, costs, focus and collection were set aside as the vertiginous Moreau Kusonski and Genton-designed building with its striking exoskeleton drew a wave of excitement and wonderment from a crush of curious visitors, just some of the 20,000 people who were expected to cross the threshold over its opening weekend. A dragon dance on the opening day. James Brickwood Without exception, visitors were taken aback by the ambition and spectacle of the marquee opening exhibition: Task Eternal, an exploration of space and flight in four chapters. Queues were longest in the museum’s only dedicated children’s show, The Dark, with its meteor tunnel, night forest and spaceship, for Es Devlin’s The Turning which has timed entry. The only slight grizzle at The Dark was that phones had to be placed out of sight in a sealed pouch to encourage sensory engagement.

Advertisement

Delighted children paddled bare-footed in the shallow pond of the Indigenous show, Overflow, while panoramic views from the CBD to the Blue Mountains through the soaring glass windows drew onlookers and selfies. Most visitors said they would be back. It was former premier Mike Baird who announced bombshell plans to relocate the Powerhouse in the state’s most populous region weeks out from the 2015 election. Premier Chris Minns and visiting schoolchildren from far western NSW cut the ribbon. Audrey Richardson Hours before opening, the Powerhouse Parramatta was ready for visitors. Audrey Richardson But it was Labor Premier Chris Minns who cut the ribbon on the monumental project – after a Coalition backflip on closure of its Ultimo home – with help from 18 visiting students of Menindee Central School, the museum’s first overnighting students.

Advertisement

Minns declared the museum “open for business” shortly after 10am, later admitting that Labor’s historic opposition to the project had been “wrong” and the museum would be “city shaping”. “I think it’s important that I acknowledge that at different points over the last few years, when we were in opposition, we were sceptical about this project. We wanted a cultural institution in western Sydney, but we did criticise this project. We were wrong. This is fantastic. This is going to be great for western Sydney. It’s going to be great for NSW.” Related Article Analysis

Development The face missing from the opening of the new Powerhouse Arts minister John Graham acknowledged the role of the museum’s absent chief executive – Lisa Havilah, who was stood down 72 days ago pending the outcome of a formal misconduct investigation – prompting cheers from members of the audience. Appointed in 2019 and a critical force in the building’s design, fitout and shows, Havilah was not invited to the event. “There’s an investigation taking place, and we need to make sure that’s done,” Minns later said. “But I think that you can do two things at the same time. You can pay tribute to the enormous work that Lisa and others have put into the institution while respecting the need for an independent investigation.”

Advertisement

Asked if the inquiry would be resolved quickly, Graham said: “One of the issues with that process is people have got a right to be able to contribute more material and ask for more time. We will not short-circuit that process.” The museum is staging five shows, all of which are free except for Task Eternal, where visitors aged over 16 pay $30. Accessing James Turrell’s Shangri La (Over the Hump) within that exhibition will cost an additional $10. The Roselands shopping centres. “raindrop fountain”, part of The Mall, one of the new museum’s exhibitions. Sam Mooy Visitors explore the exhibition. Audrey Richardson After weeks of prevarication, the museum’s open hours for exhibition shows from November 30 were confirmed as 10am to 5pm, with Friday late entry, a retreat on original plans to run the Powerhouse as a 24-hour museum, with nightly events, overnight stays and apartments for visiting artists and scientists.

Advertisement

The opening of 30 serviced apartments built on the top floor of the Powerhouse Parramatta and fitted out at a cost of more than $3 million has been delayed. These are to cater for visiting artists and scientists, but the logistics and management remains under review. Powerhouse says it has secured 18 contracted bookings for its commercial spaces, through to June 2027, from business, industry, cultural and government organisations. The announcement on the museum’s opening hours raises questions about the size of the workforce required now that the museum will be brought in line with all other cultural institutions. Visitors streamed into the new museum. James Brickwood Minns committed to funding the museum’s operations sufficiently to enable it to live up to its potential. “It’s not cheap, and it does cost taxpayer money, but we believe this is an investment in the future. The fixed costs of this beautiful building mean that you’ve got to have world-class exhibitions inside their halls.” Powerhouse Trust president David Borger lobbied for western Sydney’s first state significant cultural institution. “As a young bloke growing up in Parramatta I walked past this site … on my way to school. There was a car park here. It was the ugliest building on the Parramatta River, and never in my wildest dreams would I have thought that we’d actually have this magnificent cultural institution built. We haven’t done anything like this, frankly, since the Opera House. But there’s a new house in town.”

Advertisement

The unfurling of a banner declaring the Powerhouse “not a museum” and “vale Willow Grove” alluded to two of the many controversies which have embroiled the project – the demolition of historic building Willow Grove, which made way for the redevelopment, and ongoing controversy over its remit and treatment of its priceless collection. Long-time heritage advocate Suzette Meade said she was not surprised by the action given the street protests in 2021 and the extent of feeling. “Five years after the demolition of Willow Grove, the community’s blood still boils over this project. The NSW government underestimated the damage it caused, the disrespect it showed and how deeply it disenfranchised the people of Parramatta. We will never forget.” Protest banners reminding Sydney of the heritage building that was demolished to build the new museum in Parramatta. Audrey Richardson The day began with an official ribbon-cutting ceremony, kicked off by a Welcome to Country, with seven of the eight children who were present for the 2019 groundbreaking ceremony attending as young adults. The proceedings were watched by some of the museum’s youngest collaborators, Thoedore Bui, Jason Cilia and Tyler Pham Luu, all aged four, who donated toys to the museum’s dedicated children’s show, The Dark. Following the Australian Museum opening in 1827, major state arts spending had remained clustered east of Sydney Olympic Park, and this project marks a reshaping of Parramatta and a less CBD-centric arts scene.

Advertisement

For arts advocate John Kirkman, who was on the advisory committee that had lobbied for funding equity in western Sydney, the Powerhouse stands alongside the Sydney Opera House as an institutional project that is both controversial and transformative. Related Article Visual story

Development Inside Sydney’s newest billion-dollar house “I take a broader view on these massive cultural developments,” he says. “They are rare, transformative, and signal something profoundly positive about cultural production and public investment. A Sydney without the Opera House is inconceivable today – it delivered far more than anyone anticipated at the time. This is that same kind of moment.” For Kirkman, the investment holds generational weight. “Growing up in Granville, I lived in a fibro house with no books and no art, but I loved the idea of a museum,” he recalls. “I used to take the train to the Powerhouse at Ultimo and spend the day there. It was amazing because it was so far removed from my immediate world. This new institution has the power to open up the world to so many young people in that exact same way.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. A family trust linked to developer Lancini Property Group has handed the LNP a six-figure donation, just two months after being awarded rights to prime state-owned waterfront land in Brisbane. Electoral Commission of Queensland disclosure logs reveal the Lancini Family Discretionary Trust’s $100,000 donation, declared on Thursday, was the single biggest contribution to the party since the Crisafulli government scrapped the state’s developer donation ban. In September, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie announced 13 luxury towers, housing up to 5000 people, would be built on the site as part of a residential mixed-use precinct. Lancini Property Group is one of five companies to develop the Hamilton Northshore site. Queensland state government Economic Development Queensland selected five separate developers, including Lancini Property Group, to develop the six-hectare site, expected to include 2200 units, a shopping centre, hotel, childcare facility and medical services.

Lancini Property Group chairman Laurence Lancini sits on the GIICA board and has previously told The Australian his Hamilton interests were on the authority’s conflict of interest register. Jokes radiate throughout Queensland’s cricket scene when it comes to Jem Ryan, though there would be few quips that are as flattering as what the blossoming paceman receives. His teammates often refer to him as “Temu Barrel” or “Baby Barrel”, according to former New Zealand international Hamish Bennett, for his similarities to Test sensation Scott Boland in how he goes about his business on the field. Ryan is poised to lead the next generation of fast bowlers. AAPIMAGE “He sort of possesses [the Boland traits] – he bowls over perpendicular, he can move the ball and wing the ball both ways if he wants, but he just focuses on control, which is one of his strengths,” the Bulls bowling coach told this masthead. “He doesn’t try to get too fancy or too clever, he just repeats and repeats ball after ball, and it’s really impressive to watch. I think he’s probably someone who is just a born bowler.”

Advertisement

Bennett laughed that Ryan perhaps considered himself to be a budding AFL star before honing his focus on cricket, given his older brother Samson managed 31 games for the Richmond Tigers between 2021 and 2026. The latter has since inked a contract with the North Melbourne Kangaroos. But the 22-year-old has pursued his ambition to become a future spearhead of the Baggy Green, as he leads a contingent of six Queensland quicks all aged 22 or under eager to announce themselves as potential successors to Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Pat Cummins. Related Article Test cricket Australia’s batting is under siege. An unheralded candidate has thrust his hand up While Ryan had battled some stress-related injuries in his juniors, Bennett said those setbacks had not been cricket-caused, until he suffered a side strain in the Bulls’ drawn clash with Victoria at the Gabba last week. That concern kept him from bowling on day four, having taken three wickets in each innings – including the scalps of former Test batsmen Peter Handscomb and Marcus Harris in each knock, and international squad member for the South Africa series Sam Harper in the second dig.

Advertisement

Ryan has now claimed a wicket in each of his Sheffield Shield innings across six matches, with Bulls interim skipper Mitch Swepson revealing changes to the youngster’s run-up had been key in reaping rewards. “I know that was one thing this preseason he worked a lot on, and the more preseasons you do the stronger you get, the more you trust your body, and the more you get your recovery right, so he’s ticking all those boxes,” Swepson said. “You’d think he’s been playing for seasons, he just locks in, and it’s unfortunate he’s done a little injury – we’ll see how long that puts him out for. Hopefully, he gets back soon because he’s in a lovely rhythm at the moment … and adds a lot to our attack. “You’re seeing out there a pretty formidable bowler when he gets it right.” Loading

Advertisement

Bennett elaborated that run-up tweak came back to shortening his charge, having approached the crease in a “static” fashion only to have now found greater rhythm. But Ryan is not alone in pushing his credentials as a man for national selectors to watch once the nation’s superstar trio draw the curtain on their careers. Within the Bulls’ ranks is an emerging cartel – Charles Lachmund, Callum Vidler, Thomas Straker, Tom Balkin, Ollie Patterson and Ryan – who are all in the fledgling stages of their professional tenures, and bring versatile assets to the state set-up. “The great thing is they’ve all got different character traits and different skills. Some possess pace, some possess height, some swing it, some nip it, some are bounce bowlers, and some rely purely on air speed,” Bennett said.

Advertisement

“I think the variety of the bowlers is probably the most exciting bit; not one of them is the same, and when you go against different state teams it’s always nice having that variation in your attack and those subtle differences.” Injuries have derailed several of the group throughout the fledgling stages of their careers, with Vidler – who regularly clocks speeds of well faster than 140km/h – slowly being managed back from stress fractures in his back, having not been sighted on the field since March 2025. Related Article Analysis

Steve Smith Steve Smith’s wizardry can be developed. These cricket experts reveal how Lachmund, meanwhile, took 12 wickets at an average of 16.33 at this year’s Under-19s One-Day World Cup and got his first opportunity with Queensland’s Second XI this summer. Bennett hinted the teenager – capable of bowling regularly beyond 140km/h – would be eased towards higher honours. “The delicate thing with these young guys who bowl fast is making sure you slowly expose them. White ball cricket is ruthless when you miss your area, the margin for error is small … and then the demands for Shield cricket are so hard physically,” Bennett said.

“It’s just about trying to time your run perfectly with whatever format he is going to debut in.” Bennett said Vidler was working towards hitting top flight around Christmas during the Brisbane Heat’s Big Bash League campaign, referring to the red-haired tearaway as a “Formula One car – a young 21-year-old kid who can bowl 150km/h out-swingers”. “He’s looked really impressive in the nets, we clocked him the other day at 145km/h, so he’s going now, but he’s a Formula 1 car – you have to slowly get all your mechanics right, and sometimes the slight misalignment or misjudgement can set you back a couple of weeks,” Bennett said. “He actually got quite sick in the winter, so he had three weeks off training which really set us back. title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.
